drills.title: Missing Denominator
drills.prompt: The VP of Sales says East is our strongest region and wants to move two reps there from West. Based on Exhibit A, do you agree?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Closed-won deals by region, FY2024 (count)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that deal counts cannot be compared across regions because team sizes differ — East 510 deals on 21 managers is about 24 per manager, West 290 on 9 is about 32; (2) states that win rate cannot be computed at all from this exhibit because the number of leads or opportunities per region is absent, and that 510/1,600 is a share of wins, not a win rate; (3) names revenue per manager as the comparable measure — West about $1.68M, East about $0.70M; (4) refuses the reallocation on that basis rather than on "not enough data" in general.

reference.en:
- Naive: East has the most deals won, 510 of 1,600 = 31.9%, so it is the strongest region and deserves more reps. That is the honest first read of the table.
- Correct: the regions are not comparable head to head, because East fields 21 managers against West's 9. Per manager it is about 24 deals in East against about 32 in West. In money the gap is wider still: West brings 290 x $52,000 / 9 = about $1.68M per manager, East 510 x $29,000 / 21 = about $0.70M.
- What the exhibit cannot tell you: a win rate. That needs leads or opportunities per region, and the table has no such column. 510/1,600 is a share of the wins, not a rate.
- Last mile: the missing figure is the number of leads per region; it is what unlocks win rate = wins / leads, the only measure of regional strength. Until it exists, moving two reps from West to East moves them from the more productive region to the less productive one.

drills.title: Percent of What
drills.prompt: Our online channel share rose from 25% to 28% of revenue. The team calls it a win. Do you agree?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue mix by channel

lines: **Footnote to the exhibit:** company revenue FY2023 = **$200M**, FY2024 = **$180M**.

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) notices the base changed — company revenue fell from $200M to $180M, so a share is being taken of a shrinking base; (2) converts both shares to money: online $50.0M to $50.4M, growth of +0.8%, not a three-point gain in the business; (3) identifies Grocery as the source of the decline — $76M to $61.2M, about −19.5%; (4) concludes that the online result does not offset the fall and cannot justify a larger online budget on its own.

reference.en:
- Naive: the online share rose from 25% to 28% of revenue, three points up, so the channel is winning. The footnote is easy to skip.
- Correct: the base moved. Company revenue fell from $200M to $180M, so the same share is a share of less. In money, online went from $50.0M to $50.4M — up 0.8%, not up three points.
- Where the loss actually sits: Grocery fell from 38% to 34% of a smaller total, which is $76M to $61.2M, about −19.5%. That single channel accounts for most of the $20M decline.
- Last mile: 28% of $180M = $50.4M against 25% of $200M = $50.0M, so the three points of share are worth $0.4M. Meanwhile $200M − $180M = $20M of revenue is simply gone, and $0.4M does not cover it. Online held its money while every other channel gave some up, which is a relative success worth naming — but it is not a win, and the decision on the online budget cannot rest on this figure.

drills.title: Straight Line, Bumpy Road
drills.prompt: The CFO reports "steady 7% annual growth over five years" and proposes to extend the current plan unchanged. What do you make of it?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue, FY2019–FY2024 ($M)

lines: *Revenue = customers × average contract in every year (checkable by multiplying).*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) computes the five-year CAGR at about 6.96% and states that it is arithmetically right; (2) walks the series year by year and names the 2021 to 2022 fall of about −23.61%, from $396.0M to $302.5M; (3) states that recovery ran at a different rate — 2022 to 2024 CAGR about 17.83% — so there are two phases, not one trend; (4) notes that customers fell from 15,000 to 11,000 and are still at 14,000, so the 2024 figure rests on price ($30,000 against $26,400), not on volume; (5) refuses to extend the plan unchanged on that basis.

reference.en:
- Naive: revenue went from $300.0M to $420.0M in five years, a compound rate of 6.96%, reported as a steady 7%, so growth looks steady and the plan can simply be extended.
- Correct: the rate is right and the word "steady" is not. Between 2021 and 2022 revenue fell from $396.0M to $302.5M, about −23.61%. The recovery that followed ran at about 17.83% a year. One number is covering two different periods.
- What drove the recovery: not customers. The base went 15,000 to 11,000 and is back only to 14,000. Average contract went $24,000 to $30,000 over the six years, and $26,400 to $30,000 since the trough. The 2024 revenue is a price story.
- Last mile: a plan extended "as is" assumes the past five years were one process. They were a fall and a price-led recovery, with volume still below its 2021 peak. Before extending anything, ask what caused the 2022 drop and whether the price path has further to run.

drills.title: The Missing Fifteen
drills.prompt: Our CEO says we are the clear market leader with 38% share and wants to raise prices. What does Exhibit A tell you?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Subscription revenue share, national market ($700M total)

lines: **Form: F3 — stacked structure.** The $700M market is broken down into a "player → tariff plan" stack. The remainder of the market is **physically absent** from the stack — it is neither labelled nor named.
*Note: shares are calculated against the total national subscription video market, $700M.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) adds the shares — 38 + 27 + 20 = 85 — and states that 15% of the market, about $105M, is not shown at all; (2) states that Wexmoor's share is 38% of the whole $700M market, about $266M, and that renormalising to the 85% shown would overstate it as about 44.7%; (3) notes that the unshown $105M is comparable in size to Rival B at $140M, so it may be a fragmented competitor or a substitute; (4) makes the pricing decision conditional on identifying that remainder rather than approving the rise.

reference.en:
- Naive: three players are shown, we hold the largest slice at 38%, so we lead and can price up. Some candidates go further and renormalise to the shares actually drawn, 38 + 27 + 20 = 85, reading our slice as 38 / 85 = about 44.7%.
- Correct: the shares add to 85%. The missing 15% — about $105M of a $700M market — is not drawn, not labelled and not named anywhere in the exhibit. It has to be found by adding.
- Why it matters: $105M is not a rounding remainder. Rival B, a named player, is 20% of $700M = $140M — the same order of size. Whatever holds it is a competitor the size of a named player, and nothing here says whether it is one firm, many small ones, or a substitute product.
- Last mile: our share is 38% of $700M = $266M, not 38 / 85 = 44.7% of the slice that happens to be drawn. Raising price hands volume to whoever holds that 15%, and right now we cannot say who that is. Identify the remainder first; the price decision depends on it.
- Worth noting alongside: our ARPU is already $106.40 a year against $90.00 and $87.50 for the two named rivals. There is less headroom above the market than the share alone suggests.

drills.title: Four Rows Too Many
drills.prompt: We must close a $6M annual cost gap. Attrition is the suspected driver. Where would you focus, and why there?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Staff attrition, FY2024

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that leavers must be weighted by replacement cost rather than counted — Field ops 120 x $35,000 = $4.20M, Administrative 270 x $3,000 = $0.81M; (2) states that Field ops is about 63.0% of total replacement cost, $4.20M of about $6.66M, while having the smallest headcount at 2,000; (3) states that Field ops alone covers about 70.0% of the $6M gap and that Field ops plus Education reaches about 85.0%; (4) recommends concentrating retention on Field ops rather than on the largest headcount.

reference.en:
- Naive: Administrative has the most leavers, 270 of 755, and the largest headcount, so that is where the attrition problem is. Counting people is the obvious first move.
- Correct: a leaver is not a leaver. Weighted by replacement cost, Field ops is 120 x $35,000 = $4.20M and Administrative is 270 x $3,000 = $0.81M. Field ops is about 63.0% of the roughly $6.66M total while employing 2,000 people against Administrative's 9,000.
- Against the target: Field ops alone is about 70.0% of the $6M gap. Adding Education takes it to about 85.0%. Maintenance and Administrative together move the number very little, whatever their headcount.
- Last mile: put the retention programme on Field ops. Spreading it across all four categories spends most of the effort where a saved leaver is worth $3,000 instead of $35,000. The attrition rate points the same way — about 6.0% in Field ops against 2.5% to 4.0% elsewhere — so the problem is both concentrated and expensive.

drills.title: Richer per Unit
drills.prompt: A PE fund is looking at Halden. Management points to a 30% revenue share versus 25% unit share as proof of brand strength. Do you buy that argument?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Market shares, FY2024
Exhibit B — Market totals, FY2024

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) reads the share gap as a price difference rather than as brand strength — implied price $180,000 for Halden against $140,000 for competitors; (2) states the premium with its base named — about +28.57% against competitors, or about +20.00% against the market average of $150,000 — and does not mix the two; (3) notes that 62% of sales run through tenders, where price decides, so the premium is exposed rather than protected; (4) frames the answer for the fund as a margin risk rather than as evidence of a brand asset.

reference.en:
- Naive: we take 30% of the revenue on 25% of the units, therefore customers pay more for our name, therefore the brand is strong. The two shares sit next to each other and invite exactly this reading.
- Correct: the gap between the two shares is arithmetic, not evidence. With a $900,000,000 market and 6,000 machines, the average machine is $150,000. Halden's 30% of revenue on 25% of units implies $180,000 a machine; the rest of the market implies $140,000. The gap says our price is higher. It says nothing about why.
- Name the base: +28.57% is against competitors, +20.00% is against the market average. Both are correct and they are not the same number; quoting one while meaning the other is where this argument usually goes wrong.
- Last mile: 62% of the market is sold through tenders, where the decision is made on price. A premium that has to survive a tender every time is a risk to margin, not a moat. Warranty claims run at 4.1 per 100 machines against 3.8 for competitors, so the premium is not being paid for measured quality either. For a fund, this is a compression risk to underwrite, not a brand asset to pay for.

drills.title: Both Up, Total Down
drills.prompt: Both our sales segments improved conversion at every stage of the funnel, yet the CRO says overall win rate fell. Is someone wrong?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Sales funnel by segment (F6: conversion cascade)
Exhibit B — Segment economics

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) confirms both readings are arithmetically right rather than picking a side — every stage improved in both segments (Enterprise 50.00 to 55.00, 60.00 to 64.00, 80.00 to 81.82; SMB 40.00 to 44.00, 50.00 to 52.00, 40.00 to 41.96) and no step got worse; (2) computes the aggregate as 1,200/10,000 = 12.00% against 1,728/16,000 = 10.80% and states the move as −1.20 percentage points, not −1.20% — answering "fell 1.20%" is a unit error and fails this item; (3) names the mix shift as the cause: Enterprise share of leads 25.00% to 6.25%, while Enterprise converts 28.80% against SMB's 9.60%, so the aggregate is weighted by lead volume and not by lead quality; (4) does not treat the two years as comparable in segment weight, and does not read SMB's lead growth from 7,500 to 15,000 as the good-news driver; (5) points the fix at Enterprise lead flow (1,000 against 2,500), not at conversion. Bonus, not required for credit: sizes it as 1,500 lost leads x 28.80% x $240,000 = about $103.7M of pipeline never created.

reference.en:
- Naive: every stage of both funnels converts better in FY2024 than in FY2023 — Enterprise 50.00% to 55.00%, 60.00% to 64.00%, 80.00% to 81.82%; SMB 40.00% to 44.00%, 50.00% to 52.00%, 40.00% to 41.96%. Not one step got worse, so the CRO must be looking at the wrong number.
- Correct: nobody is wrong. Enterprise takes 600 of 2,500 leads to a win in FY2023, 24.00%, and 288 of 1,000 in FY2024, 28.80%; SMB goes from 600 of 7,500, 8.00%, to 1,440 of 15,000, 9.60%. Both segments improved. But the aggregate is 1,200 wins on 10,000 leads = 12.00% against 1,728 wins on 16,000 leads = 10.80%. Every part rose and the total fell.
- Why the total can fall: mix. Enterprise converts 28.80% against SMB's 9.60%, and Enterprise supplied 2,500 of 10,000 leads, 25.00%, in FY2023 but only 1,000 of 16,000, 6.25%, in FY2024. The aggregate weights the two funnels by lead volume, not by lead quality, so weight moving to the weaker funnel drags the total down while both funnels are getting stronger.
- Watch the unit: the overall win rate went 12.00% to 10.80%. That is a fall of 1.20 percentage points, not a fall of 1.20%; relative to a 12.00% base the decline is 10%. Reporting it as "down 1.20%" names a different and much smaller event: a relative fall of 1.20% would have left the rate at 11.86%, not at 10.80%.
- Last mile: the drop is not a sales-execution problem, because execution improved at every step of both funnels. It is a demand-generation problem one level up: Enterprise leads collapsed from 2,500 to 1,000, a factor of 2.5. At a 28.80% win rate and an average deal of $240,000, the 1,500 missing leads are about $103.7M of pipeline that was never created. Fix the Enterprise lead flow; the conversion cascade needs no fixing at all.

drills.title: Two Lists, One Choice
drills.prompt: We need to pick one segment to enter. Exhibit A shows the market, Exhibit B our capabilities. Which segment, and what would you expect to capture?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Market structure ($700M total)
Exhibit B — Our capability fit (internal assessment)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that neither exhibit answers the question alone — Exhibit A gives size, Exhibit B gives reach — and that the two percentage columns are different in kind, so they must be multiplied rather than compared; (2) computes expected revenue for all four segments off the single $700M base: Discount $56,000,000, Premium $73,500,000, Value $96,250,000, Natural $35,000,000; (3) picks Value at $96,250,000 and says explicitly that it wins although it is neither the largest share (Discount, 40%) nor the fastest growing (Natural, 35% a year); (4) rejects Discount on capability — 20% distribution coverage against a $280.0M market — not on size; (5) does not pick Natural on growth, and preferably notes that production readiness is "no", so entry carries capital spend that neither exhibit prices.

reference.en:
- Naive: Discount is the biggest block on Exhibit A, 40% of the $700M market, so enter Discount. The other quick read picks Natural, growing 35% a year, the fastest of the four. Both are honest first reads of Exhibit A alone.
- Correct: neither exhibit answers the question by itself. Exhibit A sizes the prize, Exhibit B says how much of it we can actually reach, and the two percentages are different in kind — share of market against share of distribution covered. The answer is the product. Discount: 40% x $700M = $280.0M of market, 20% coverage, $56,000,000 expected. Premium: 15% x $700M = $105.0M, 70% coverage, $73,500,000. Value: 25% x $700M = $175.0M, 55% coverage, $96,250,000. Natural: 20% x $700M = $140.0M, 25% coverage, $35,000,000.
- Why the biggest segment loses: Discount is the largest market at 40% x $700M = $280.0M and still returns the second-lowest expected revenue, because 20% coverage strands four fifths of it. Size without reach is not opportunity.
- Why the fastest segment loses: Natural grows 35% a year and lands last at $35,000,000 on 25% coverage. Production readiness there is "no", so entry also needs capital spend that neither exhibit prices. Growth sits in its own column and says nothing about attainability.
- Last mile: enter Value. It is neither the largest (Discount, 40%) nor the fastest (Natural, 35% a year), but 25% x $700M x 55% = $96,250,000 of expected addressable revenue, $22,750,000 clear of Premium at $73,500,000, the closest alternative.

drills.title: Volume Here, Price There
drills.prompt: We are choosing which cinema format to partner with. Which format delivers the most revenue, and how much?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Cinema capacity by format
Exhibit B — Ticket economics

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) builds daily tickets from Exhibit A as screens x showings x seats x occupancy rather than reading screen count as size — Single-screen 1,200 x 4 x 150 x 50% = 360,000 and Multiplex 750 x 6 x 200 x 40% = 360,000, an exact tie on volume, Premium 48,600; (2) states that revenue needs the Exhibit B price on top of that volume — $360,000, $1,080,000 and $388,800 a day; (3) names Multiplex as the answer at $1,080,000 of $1,828,800, about 59.1% of daily revenue, on 750 screens against Single-screen's 1,200, or 37.5% fewer; (4) rejects both the largest-network read and the highest-price read, noting that Premium's $8.00 ticket yields only $388,800 because the base is 48,600 tickets; (5) does not treat bar share or distributor commission as revenue.

reference.en:
- Naive: Single-screen runs 1,200 screens against 750 for Multiplex and 180 for Premium, by far the largest network, so it must bring in the most revenue. The rival first read is the opposite one: Premium charges $8.00 a ticket against $1.00, so the money must sit there.
- Correct: neither screens nor price is revenue on its own. Capacity has to be carried all the way to tickets: screens x showings x seats x occupancy. Single-screen gives 1,200 x 4 x 150 x 50% = 360,000 tickets a day. Multiplex gives 750 x 6 x 200 x 40% = 360,000, exactly the same. Premium gives 180 x 5 x 90 x 60% = 48,600.
- What price then does: with volume tied, the ticket line from the second exhibit decides everything. Single-screen 360,000 x $1.00 = $360,000 a day, Multiplex 360,000 x $3.00 = $1,080,000, Premium 48,600 x $8.00 = $388,800. Total daily revenue is $1,828,800.
- Why the expensive format loses: the highest ticket in the exhibit, $8.00, returns $388,800, about 21.3% of the $1,828,800, because Premium sells 48,600 tickets against 360,000. The price edge over Multiplex is a factor of 2.67 ($8.00 against $3.00); the volume shortfall is a factor of 7.41 (48,600 against 360,000), and the larger factor wins.
- On the remaining columns: bar share and distributor commission — Premium 35% and 55% against Multiplex 28% and 50% — are margin items, not revenue. On a full profit view they would narrow the gap to Multiplex, not reverse it.
- Last mile: volume is identical across the two large formats and price is not, so Multiplex delivers $1,080,000 of the $1,828,800 daily revenue, about 59.1%, while operating 750 screens against Single-screen's 1,200 — 37.5% fewer screens for three times the money. Partner with Multiplex.

drills.title: Nothing Wrong Here
drills.prompt: Our strategy deck claims we hold an 18% share of this market. Verify it and tell me whether the claim stands.

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Market revenue by segment, FY2024

lines: **Form: F5 — a "segment × price tier" matrix, data in the cells.**
Our revenue, $M — by the same cells:
*Note: the salon services market is limited to four price segments and three geography types; the sample contains no other categories.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) adds both matrices instead of looking for a printed total — market $300M, our revenue $54M; (2) computes $54M / $300M = 18.00% and states that the 18% claim in the deck is confirmed; (3) rejects the idea of a hidden segment on the ground that the four segments themselves sum to $300M ($120M, $90M, $60M, $30M), not on the ground that the note says the sample is complete; (4) rejects the average ticket — $74 in the capital against $31 in small towns — as irrelevant to a share computed on revenue; (5) says explicitly that there is no trap in this exhibit and why, rather than manufacturing a correction; (6) offers the uneven cell-level share as the next question — mid in the capital, 9 of 33 = 27.3%, against premium in small towns, 1 of 17 = 5.9%.

reference.en:
- Naive: a share claim laid over a matrix invites suspicion, so the reflex is to hunt for what is missing — a segment left off the grid, a base that needs renormalising, or a price effect hiding in the $74 capital ticket against $31 in small towns. None of that is here, and hunting for it is the error this exhibit is built to catch.
- Correct: add the cells and the claim holds. Market is 62+41+17+33+38+19+14+25+21+5+11+14 = $300M, our revenue is 11+6+1+9+8+4+3+5+4+1+1+1 = $54M, and $54M / $300M = 18.00%. The deck is right as written.
- Why there is no missing remainder: the four segments close on the same total — premium $120M, mid $90M, economy $60M, express $30M, which sum to $300M. The exhibit prints no total row, so this has to be added rather than read; that addition is the whole of the work.
- Why the operations rows do not disturb it: salons run 24, 39 and 25 across the three geographies, average ticket $74, $48 and $31, chair utilisation 71%, 64% and 58%. Ticket and utilisation are already inside the revenue figures, so they describe how the revenue was earned; they cannot bend a ratio taken on revenue itself.
- What is genuinely uneven is the share underneath the average: 15.00% in premium, 23.33% in mid, 20.00% in economy, 10.00% in express. At cell level the spread is wider — mid in the capital is 9 of 33 = 27.3%, premium in small towns is 1 of 17 = 5.9%.
- Last mile: the answer is that the claim stands and needs no correction, and that has to be said in those words rather than softened into a caveat. The follow-up is the spread, not the headline: why mid in the capital, 9 of 33, sits at 27.3% while premium in small towns, 1 of 17, sits at 5.9%.

drills.title: Small Base, Big Noise
drills.prompt: Product leadership wants to double the Analytics team, arguing it is our fastest-growing product. Does Exhibit A support that?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue bridge FY2023 → FY2024 ($M)

lines: *Note: each driver's contribution is calculated against its own FY2023 base; the bases sum to total FY2023 revenue.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) separates growth rate from growth contribution and states that Analytics' 180.00% is a rate measured against a $5M base, not a claim on dollars; (2) computes Analytics' share of the $48M increase as $9M / $48M = 18.75%, and Cloud suite's as $27M / $48M = 56.25%, three times larger; (3) states that the equal-height +9 bars for Legacy platform and Analytics represent 5.00% and 180.00% growth respectively, so bar height in this waterfall says nothing about rate; (4) redirects the headcount to Cloud suite, or at minimum refuses to double Analytics on the strength of its growth rate alone; (5) does not treat Analytics as the fastest-growing product in any sense that justifies the ask. Bonus, not required: notes Analytics has 50 customers at a $100k average contract against Cloud suite's 450 at $200k, so the constraint is buyers, not price. Penalise any forward projection that reapplies 180.00% to the $5M base instead of the $14M base Analytics ends FY2024 with.

reference.en:
- Naive: Analytics add-on grew 180.00% ($9M on a $5M base), the fastest rate on the exhibit by a wide margin, so it is the fastest-growing product and the team should be doubled. The rate is arithmetically correct, which is what makes the read tempting.
- Correct: a rate off a small base does not buy headcount; dollars do. Total revenue grew $48M, from $312M to $360M. Analytics contributed $9M of that, 18.75%. Cloud suite contributed $27M, 56.25% — three times as much — while growing at only 30.00%, because it was growing on a $90M base rather than a $5M one. The two lines answer different questions, and the one product leadership is asking is the dollar question.
- On reading the waterfall: the bars for Legacy platform and Analytics are the same height, both +9, which invites the reading that they matter equally. They do not carry the same information. Against their own bases those same +9 bars are 5.00% growth and 180.00% growth. Bar height in this chart is contribution only; rate is invisible in it and has to be computed from the base column.
- On the ceiling under Analytics: it serves 50 customers at a $100k average contract, the smallest customer base of any line on the exhibit. Cloud suite has 450 customers at $200k. Doubling an Analytics team scales capacity to sell, but the binding constraint on a $5M line with 50 accounts is how many buyers exist, not how fast the team can reach them.
- What a forward view does and does not change: the small-base effect works in Analytics' favour next year too, and the argument has to be made against the FY2024 bases, not the FY2023 ones. Analytics exits FY2024 at 5 + 9 = $14M; another 180.00% year on that is about $25.2M. Cloud suite exits at 90 + 27 = $117M; another 30.00% year is about $35.1M. Cloud suite still contributes more, but the gap narrows from 3.0x to about 1.39x. That narrowing, not this year's rate, is the only serious case for funding Analytics — and it holds only if the rate holds.
- Last mile: on the evidence in front of us, of the $48M of growth Analytics produced $9M and Cloud suite $27M, so the headcount belongs on Cloud suite today. The question that would change the answer is not how fast Analytics grew, it is how many buyers exist beyond the current 50 customers — because only a rate that survives on a $14M base makes the doubling pay, and nothing on this exhibit says it will.

drills.title: Quarters and Years
drills.prompt: The board packet says revenue is declining — the latest bar is well below the prior one. Is that right?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue ($M)

lines: *Note: the FY columns are calendar years, the Q columns are quarters of 2024. The chart axis does not distinguish the two period types.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that the periods are of two different granularities — FY2021 through FY2023 are full years, Q1 through Q4 2024 are quarters of one year — so 147 cannot be set against 504; (2) sums the four quarters to FY2024 = $519M and compares it with FY2023 at $504M, giving +2.98%, an increase and not a decline; (3) reads the within-year path 114 to 147 as rising and computes the Q4 run-rate of $588M, 13.29% above the actual $519M; (4) concludes that the board packet's declining-revenue message is wrong and reframes the question as one of growth rate — 9.54% a year across FY2021 to FY2023 against +2.98% in FY2024. Do not credit an answer that reports a fall of −70.83% off the last two bars, or that reads the four 2024 quarters as an annual trend line. Margin and store count are not required; if used, margin must be described as rising from 34.0% to 36.2%, a gain stated in percentage points rather than percent.

reference.en:
- Naive: the last bar is 147 against 504 before it, a fall of −70.83%, so revenue has collapsed. Off the axis alone, that is what the chart appears to say.
- Correct: the two bars are not the same kind of period. FY2021 through FY2023 are calendar years; Q1 through Q4 2024 are quarters of a single year. Adding the four quarters gives FY2024 = 114 + 126 + 132 + 147 = $519M against $504M in FY2023, growth of +2.98%. Revenue rose.
- Inside the year: 114, 126, 132, 147, every quarter above the one before it. Q4 annualised is 147 x 4 = $588M, 13.29% above the actual FY2024 of $519M, so the exit rate is running ahead of the year's average.
- What growth actually did: FY2021 to FY2023 compounded at 9.54% a year; FY2024 landed at +2.98%. The story is a deceleration in the growth rate, not a decline in revenue.
- Margin runs the other way: 34.0% to 36.2%, a gain of 2.2 percentage points of gross margin over the same span, with stores up from 239 to 252. Slower top-line growth is arriving alongside better quality of earnings.
- Last mile: comparing a quarter with a year manufactured the fall, so the packet's headline is wrong. FY2024 is $519M against $504M, up +2.98%, with a Q4 run-rate of $588M. Correct the packet, then put the real question to the board — why growth decelerated from 9.54% a year to +2.98% — rather than debating a decline that did not happen.

drills.title: Two Lines, One Story
drills.prompt: Marketing claims their spend drives revenue — the two move together almost perfectly. Do you accept that?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Marketing spend and revenue

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) refuses the causal claim and states that two series rising together does not establish that one drives the other; (2) names a third quantity in the exhibit moving with both — clinics go 240 to 425, about 12.11% a year; (3) computes revenue per clinic and states it is close to flat, $1,291.7k in 2019 against $1,317.6k in 2024, about +2.0% over five years, so revenue growth tracks network expansion rather than marketing effectiveness; (4) states that marketing grew faster than revenue, about 25.26% a year against about 12.56%, so spend per clinic rose while return per clinic did not; (5) names a specific alternative explanation — a common driver (network expansion) or reverse causality (budget set as a share of revenue); (6) proposes a test that separates the explanations, such as comparing revenue at like-for-like clinics open since 2019 under different levels of marketing spend, or finding clinics where the budget moved out of proportion to revenue. Do not credit "correlation is not causation" without both a named alternative and a discriminating test.

reference.en:
- Naive: marketing went from $12M to $37M and revenue from $310M to $560M, moving together year after year with no exception, so the spend must be driving the revenue. Synchrony this clean is the most persuasive thing in the table, and it is the honest first read.
- Correct: a third column moves with both. Clinics go 240 to 425, about 12.11% a year, and revenue compounds at about 12.56% a year — almost the same rate. The network is growing, and revenue is growing with it.
- Revenue per clinic settles it: $310M over 240 clinics is $1,291.7k, $560M over 425 clinics is $1,317.6k. That is about +2.0% across five years. Whatever the extra spend bought, it did not raise what an average clinic earns.
- Marketing, meanwhile, compounds at about 25.26% a year against revenue's 12.56%. Spend per clinic is climbing steeply while return per clinic is flat — the opposite of what an effective-marketing story predicts.
- Reverse causality is at least as plausible as the claim. If the budget is set as a share of revenue, the two series move together by construction and revenue "causes" the spend, not the other way round.
- Last mile: rejecting causality is not the answer on its own. Name the alternative — network expansion as a common driver, or budget-as-a-share-of-revenue as reverse causality — and then name the test that separates them: compare revenue at like-for-like clinics open since 2019 across different levels of marketing spend, or find clinics where the budget moved out of proportion to revenue. Without that test, both stories fit the table equally well and the exhibit decides nothing.
- What the exhibit cannot tell you: whether any driver outside these five columns matters. The table's boundary is not the boundary of reality — pricing, payer mix and local competition are absent, not absent from the business.

drills.title: The Average Lies
drills.prompt: Finance reports an average collection period of 34 days and calls working capital healthy. Do you agree?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Receivables by segment

lines: *Note: the «$ per invoice» and «Share of invoices» columns are derived from the first two columns.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) identifies that the reported 34 days is a simple average across the four segments, (18 + 26 + 34 + 58) / 4 = 34.00, and not weighted by amount; (2) recomputes the amount-weighted collection period at 39.67 days and names the gap of 5.67 days; (3) states that Government carries 37.97% of the amount ($15,000,000 of $39,500,000) on 2.88% of the invoices (60 of 2,080) at the slowest 58 days, so the tail sets the aggregate; (4) states that SMB is 72.1% of invoices but only 11.39% of the amount, so working on SMB collection at 18 days barely moves working capital; (5) treats the "$ per invoice" and "Share of invoices" columns as derived from the first two columns rather than as independent evidence; (6) rejects "healthy" and directs the action at Government, not SMB. No credit if the answer accepts 34 days as sound because it matches the industry norm, or targets SMB on the strength of its 72.1% share of invoice count.

reference.en:
- Naive: the four segment figures average to (18 + 26 + 34 + 58) / 4 = 34.00 days, which matches what Finance reported, so working capital looks healthy and the question is closed.
- Correct: that is a simple average across segments, which weights a $4,500,000 SMB book and a $15,000,000 Government book equally. Weighted by amount the collection period is 39.67 days, 5.67 days longer than reported.
- Where the weight sits: Government is 60 invoices of 2,080, 2.88% of the count, but $15,000,000 of $39,500,000, 37.97% of the money, and it is the slowest to pay at 58 days. The tail sets the aggregate.
- The mirror image: SMB is 1,500 invoices, 72.1% of the count, and 11.39% of the amount. Collecting faster than the current 18 days there barely moves working capital.
- On the derived columns: "$ per invoice" and "Share of invoices" are computed from the first two columns, not independent evidence — 15,000,000 / 60 = 250,000 reproduces exactly. Reading them as separate signals is what pulls attention toward SMB.
- Last mile: on $39,500,000 of receivables a year one day is $108,219, so the 5.67 days the simple average hides are about $614k of frozen working capital. Restate the metric as an amount-weighted 39.67 days, then work Government terms and collection rather than SMB.

drills.title: Cut at Ninety
drills.prompt: The investor deck shows revenue "surging" alongside margin. What does the chart actually show?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue and margin (dual-axis)

lines: Left axis: revenue, $M — scale starts at 800
Right axis: margin, %  — scale starts at 0

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that the left axis starts at 800, not at zero, and that the apparent (952 - 800) / (840 - 800) = 3.8x jump in the bars is an artefact of that truncation; (2) gives the real revenue move as 13.33% over the five years, a CAGR of 3.18%; (3) states that the two axes follow different conventions in one picture — the left one truncated at 800, the right one running from zero — so the two series cannot be read against each other; (4) reads the margin move as 5.8 percentage points, 11.0 to 16.8, and not as 5.8%, and converts it to the relative +52.73%; (5) names profit as the series that actually moved, $92.4M to $159.9M, +73.09%, and notes it appears on neither axis; (6) refuses the deck's "surging revenue" claim on that basis rather than on presentation style in general. Do not credit an answer that reports the margin rise as 5.8%.

reference.en:
- Naive: the revenue bars roughly quadruple across the panel while the margin line climbs with them, so revenue is surging and margin is riding along. Read off the axis as drawn, the bars really do grow (952 - 800) / (840 - 800) = 3.8x.
- Correct: the left axis starts at 800, not at zero. Revenue went 840 to 952, which is 13.33% over the five years, a CAGR of 3.18%. The 3.8x is the pedestal, not the business.
- The two axes do not follow the same rule: the left one is truncated at 800, the right one runs from zero. One picture, two reading conventions, and nothing in the chart warns you which applies where.
- Margin moved 11.0 to 16.8, which is 5.8 percentage points and not 5.8%. Relative to the base it is +52.73%.
- The series that actually moved is profit: $92.4M in 2020 against $159.9M in 2024, +73.09%. It is plotted on neither axis, so the one real result in the deck is the one the chart never shows.
- Volume fell every year of the panel, 21.0 to 18.5 M bbl, while price rose $40.00 to $51.46 per barrel. Revenue is growing on price alone.
- Last mile: the truncated axis inflates the revenue story into a 3.8x climb that the data does not support — the honest figure is a 3.18% CAGR. The deck's thesis of surging revenue does not hold; the real story is margin and price, carried on a shrinking barrel count, and it reverses the moment price does.

drills.title: Exhibits Disagree
drills.prompt: Exhibit A says EBITDA grew to $92M. Exhibit B totals $72M for the same year. One of them must be wrong — which?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — EBITDA bridge FY2023 → FY2024, $M (management accounts)
Exhibit B — Reported EBITDA by segment, FY2024 ($M, statutory accounts)

lines: *Note to Exhibit B: from 1 July FY2024 the Coastal Freight division (EBITDA $20M for a full year) was classified as discontinued operations and excluded from segment reporting.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) quantifies the gap as exactly $20M ($92M − $72M) rather than describing it as "a difference"; (2) ties that $20M to the note under Exhibit B — the Coastal Freight division, $20M of full-year EBITDA, reclassified as discontinued from 1 July FY2024 and excluded from segment reporting; (3) states that neither exhibit is wrong, and that they measure different perimeters — Exhibit A the whole business at $92M, Exhibit B continuing operations at $72M, with 31 + 22 + 19 = 72 internally consistent and the bridge 84 + 12 + 9 − 4 − 15 + 6 = 92 closing on its own; (4) rejects the framing of the question — refuses to pick a "right" exhibit and instead asks which perimeter the decision needs, buy-side valuation on $72M, management performance on $92M; (5) does not credit if the candidate resolves the conflict by ranking one exhibit as more current, more granular or more analytical than the other, or by asserting a reporting error somewhere.

reference.en:
- Naive: the two exhibits cannot both be right, so pick the better one. The bridge is newer, more granular and visibly analytical, so $92M wins and the statutory table is stale. That is the reflex the question is built to trigger, and it is the wrong move — the task is not to choose a winner.
- Correct: measure the gap before judging it. $92M − $72M = $20M, and $20M is precisely the Coastal Freight EBITDA named in the note under Exhibit B, a full year of it, reclassified as discontinued from 1 July FY2024 and dropped out of segment reporting. The number is not a discrepancy, it is an identity: 72 + 20 = 92.
- Both exhibits are internally sound. The bridge closes on itself: 84 + 12 + 9 − 4 − 15 + 6 = 92, a net movement of +$8M on the FY2023 base of 84. The segment table foots: 31 + 22 + 19 = 72. Nothing is miscast in either one.
- What differs is perimeter, not accuracy. Exhibit A is the management view of the whole business; Exhibit B is the statutory view of continuing operations only. Same year, same currency, same units — different definitions of what counts as the company.
- Underneath, a second question the perimeter clash was hiding: International carries index 108 on a 13.4% margin while North carries index 104 on 14.5%. Growth and margin rank differently by segment, which is worth its own line of inquiry once the perimeter is settled.
- Last mile: the $20M is explained by perimeter, not by error, so EBITDA on continuing operations is $72M and EBITDA of the whole business is $92M — both true, neither a correction of the other. Fix the perimeter before any decision rests on the figure: a buyer prices what it acquires, $72M; a board judging management prices what management ran, $92M. And any FY2023 to FY2024 comparison has to sit on one base, or the growth reads high by the size of the divested asset.

drills.title: Whose Growth Is It
drills.prompt: Subscription grew 60% and the team wants the next budget cycle to go there. Where did our growth actually come from?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Conversion funnel, FY2024 (F6)
Exhibit B — Revenue by line ($M)

lines: *Note: «active» is defined as having made ≥1 purchase in 90 days; the funnel in Exhibit A is built on the same cohort.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) computes each line's contribution against the FY2023 total base of $250M and not against its own base — Marketplace $45M = 18.00 pp, Subscription $24M = 9.60 pp, Ads $3M = 1.20 pp — and states that the three sum to the 28.80 pp of total growth; (2) states that Marketplace supplied 62.50% of the increment against 33.33% from Subscription while growing at 25.0% against 60%, so contribution is base times rate; (3) names Subscription's 0.42M active buyers out of 3.60M, about 11.7%, as a ceiling on what the line can contribute even at an unchanged 60%; (4) does not treat the 50.0% repeat step as the bottleneck, and reads funnel stages as multiplying — 25.0% x 30.0% x 50.0% = 3.75%; (5) sends the budget to Marketplace and states the answer in percentage points, 9.60 pp against 18.00 pp, rather than in growth rates.

reference.en:
- Naive: Subscription grew 60%, the fastest of the three lines, so the next budget cycle should follow it. That is the honest first read of the growth column.
- Correct: growth belongs to the total base, not to each line's own base. Marketplace added $45M on the FY2023 total of $250M, which is 18.00 percentage points of company growth; Subscription added $24M, 9.60 pp; Ads added $3M, 1.20 pp. They sum to 28.80 pp, which is exactly the move from $250M to $322M.
- Where the growth came from: Marketplace supplied 62.50% of the $72M increment against 33.33% from Subscription, at a rate of 25.0% against 60%. Contribution is base times rate, and the bases are $180M against $40M.
- What the funnel adds: stage rates multiply, they do not add. 25.0% x 30.0% x 50.0% = 3.75% of visitors reach a repeat purchase. The 50.0% repeat step is the best rate in the chain, not the bottleneck; a point won at the 25.0% first step carries the full 48,000,000 visitors behind it, a point won at the last step carries only 3,600,000.
- What caps Subscription: it serves 0.42M of the 3.60M active buyers, about 11.7%. Holding 60% growth does not fix that; to add the $45M Marketplace added, Subscription would have to grow 112.5% on its $40M base.
- Last mile: put the budget in Marketplace. Subscription is the faster line but delivers 9.60 pp of the 28.80 pp of total growth against 18.00 pp from Marketplace, and its 0.42M active users out of 3.60M limit how far the rate can carry it.

drills.title: One Client Moves It
drills.prompt: The portfolio grew 10% year over year and leadership wants to keep the current coverage model. Does Exhibit B support that?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Portfolio revenue and client count (dual-axis)

lines: Left axis: portfolio revenue, $M — from zero
Right axis: number of clients — from zero

blocks.title: Exhibit B — Revenue by client ($M)

lines: *Note: the Δ, Δ% and portfolio share columns are derived from FY2023 and FY2024.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that the entire +$28M portfolio gain is one client — Client A went $62M to $98M, +$36M, larger than the total increase; (2) computes the portfolio excluding Client A: $218M to $210M, −$8M or about −3.67%, and states that every other line in the exhibit is negative; (3) treats the Others line as a group aggregate — it covers 36 clients in FY2023 and 34 in FY2024, so its −$3M mixes the loss of two clients with the movement of the ones that stayed, and per-client direction inside that group cannot be read from the exhibit; (4) rejects the rise in average client size from $6.83M to $7.90M as an artifact — the numerator is lifted by one outlier and the denominator fell from 41 to 39 clients, and neither cause means a stronger base; (5) refuses to keep the coverage model on that basis rather than on the aggregate +10.00% growth.

reference.en:
- Naive: the portfolio grew from $280M to $308M, +$28M or +10.00%, and average client size rose from $6.83M to $7.90M, so the base looks healthy and the coverage model can stay as it is.
- Correct: the growth is one client. Client A went from $62M to $98M, +$36M or +58.06%, which is more than the whole portfolio gain of +$28M. Strip Client A out and the portfolio falls from $218M to $210M, −$8M or about −3.67%.

Client count went 41 to 39 while all five named clients appear in both years, so Others holds 36 clients in FY2023 and 34 in FY2024. Its −$3M therefore mixes two departures with the movement of the 34 that stayed. If the two who left were worth more than $3M between them, the survivors grew on a like-for-like basis. The exhibit cannot settle it, and reading a group total as a statement about each member inside it is the same mistake as reading the portfolio total as a statement about the base.
- Why the average misleads: average client size is a derived figure and both of its inputs moved for the wrong reasons. The numerator was lifted by a single outlier and the denominator fell from 41 to 39 clients. Losing clients raises the average even when nothing improves.
- What the aggregate hides: Client A is now 31.82% of the portfolio against 22.14% a year earlier, a rise of about 9.68 percentage points. The same event that produced the growth also produced a concentration risk — if that one client leaves, two years of portfolio movement go with it.
- Last mile: the portfolio grew +$28M, but excluding Client A it lost −$8M, about −3.67%. The aggregate describes one account, not the state of the base. Keeping the coverage model unchanged is not supportable on this exhibit. The next question is what the Others line looks like on a like-for-like basis, since attrition and shrinkage call for different responses.

drills.title: Not the Same People
drills.prompt: Product says churn is 8%. Support says it is 20%. Both pulled the same month. Who is right?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Subscriber base, March 2025
Exhibit B — Composition of the base (F3: stack)

lines: *Note: the support team measures churn against the active base; everyone who cancelled in March was among those active in the last 90 days.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that the two figures are not in conflict and that neither team made an error — the numerator is the same 38,400 cancellations in both, and only the denominator differs; (2) computes both: 38,400 / 480,000 = 8.00% and 38,400 / 192,000 = 20.00%, and identifies 480,000 as the registered base and 192,000 as the base active in the last 90 days; (3) uses the note under the second exhibit — the support team measures against the active base, and everyone who cancelled in March was active in the last 90 days — rather than guessing which denominator each team used; (4) names what the exhibit does and does not split: it splits the 480,000 by activity in the last 90 days, 192,000 against 288,000, and says nothing about which accounts are billed, so the candidate must state that activity and payment are not separated in this data and that the choice of denominator cannot be settled until they are. Credit in full an answer that raises dormant-but-billed accounts among the 288,000 as the open question; do not require the candidate to assume the 288,000 produce no revenue, and do not credit an answer that asserts they produce none as if the exhibit said so; (5) does not resolve the disagreement by declaring one team wrong, by assuming the two numbers cover different periods or methods, and does not apply 20% to the registered base to produce 96,000 cancellations. Do not credit an answer that reports both percentages without naming the denominator of each. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that a 14-month average lifetime implies about 7.1% monthly churn, close to the 8.00% figure, but that this too is computed off the full base and cannot arbitrate between the denominators.

reference.en:
- Naive: 8% and 20% for the same month cannot both be true, so the two teams must be measuring different periods, or one of them made a mistake. The instinct is to referee the dispute and pick a side.
- Correct: both figures are right, and they share a numerator. Product divides 38,400 cancellations by the 480,000 registered accounts and gets 8.00%. Support divides the same 38,400 by the 192,000 accounts active in the last 90 days and gets 20.00%. Nothing was miscounted; two different questions were answered with the same cancellations on top.
- Where the answer is hiding: not in the numbers but in the note under the second exhibit. It states that support measures against the active base and that everyone who cancelled in March was among the active. Without that line the exhibit cannot be resolved at all — the composition breakdown alone does not say which denominator either team used.
- The gap between the two rates is exactly the gap between the two bases: 480,000 against 192,000 is a factor of 2.50, and 20.00% against 8.00% is the same factor of 2.50. There is no second effect to find.
- Which base should govern, and the caveat that has to travel with the answer: 192,000 active accounts are 40.00% of the 480,000 registered, and the other 288,000 — 60.00% of the base — have not been seen in 90 days. But the exhibit splits the base by activity, not by billing. It does not say whether any of those 288,000 are still being charged. If they are not, the active base is the right denominator and 20.00% is the number to manage against. If some of them are dormant but still paying, then they can still be lost, they belong in the denominator, and neither 8.00% nor 20.00% is the churn rate anyone actually wants. State the condition rather than choosing under it.
- A cross-check that does not settle it: an average lifetime of 14 months implies a theoretical monthly churn of about 7.1%, which sits close to the 8.00% figure and looks like independent support for Product. It is not. That lifetime is itself measured across the full registered base, so it inherits the same ambiguity and cannot arbitrate between the two denominators.
- What the decomposition below the active line does not do: splitting 192,000 into 58,000 daily and 134,000 occasional, or 288,000 into 201,000 dormant under a year and 87,000 over a year, changes nothing about the arithmetic. The stack is a distractor here; the only cut that matters is active against inactive, and even that cut is drawn on the wrong axis for the question.
- The classic slip to avoid: taking 20% and applying it to 480,000 to get 96,000 cancellations. That number appears nowhere and describes nothing — it multiplies a rate by the base it was not computed against.
- Last mile: churn is 20.00% against the active base and 8.00% against the registered base, and both belong in the answer, each named with its denominator. The action is not to pick one on the spot but to close the gap in the data first: ask which of the 288,000 inactive accounts are still being billed, then fix a single definition around the paying base and hold every retention target to it. Choose a definition before that answer is in hand and you have set a target against a denominator you cannot defend.

drills.prompt: Our board deck claims a 38.1% gross margin. Verify it and tell me whether the claim stands.

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue and COGS by product line ($)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) verifies the claim from the totals — ($100,000,000 - $61,900,000) / $100,000,000 = 38.10% — and states plainly that the board deck is correct; (2) checks that the lines reconcile to the totals rather than trusting the total row: revenue 44 + 31 + 18 + 7 = 100 and COGS 26.4 + 19.53 + 11.7 + 4.27 = 61.9, in $M, so there is no hidden line item; (3) tests and rejects the loss-making-line suspicion with numbers — margins are 40.00%, 37.00%, 35.00% and 39.00%, all positive, so no line is dragging the aggregate; (4) tests and rejects the hidden-price-premium suspicion with numbers — price times volume reproduces each line's stated revenue exactly (550k x $80.00 = $44,000,000; 620k x $50.00 = $31,000,000; 300k x $60.00 = $18,000,000; 175k x $40.00 = $7,000,000); (5) says explicitly that there is no trap here and why, rather than leaving the verification implicit or hedging that something might still be wrong. Do not credit an answer that recomputes 38.10% but accepts either false suspicion, and do not credit an answer that manufactures a problem to look rigorous. Bonus, not required for credit: notes the margin spread across lines is only 5 percentage points, 35.00% to 40.00%, so a mix shift is a fair next question but does not touch the 38.10% claim.

reference.en:
- Naive: a board deck handed over with the words "verify it" is assumed to be wrong. The reflex is to hunt for the line that breaks the story — a loss-making product, a price that does not match its revenue — and to report the hunt as if it were the finding.
- Correct: the claim stands. Revenue of $100,000,000 less COGS of $61,900,000 leaves $38,100,000 of gross profit, and $38,100,000 / $100,000,000 = 38.10%, exactly as stated. The verification is one subtraction and one division.
- Do not verify off the total row alone. The four lines sum to the totals they claim: revenue $44M + $31M + $18M + $7M = $100M, and COGS $26.4M + $19.53M + $11.7M + $4.27M = $61.9M. Nothing sits outside the four lines, so the aggregate is not concealing a fifth item.
- The loss-making-line suspicion fails on the numbers. Line A runs at 40.00%, Line B at 37.00%, Line C at 35.00% and Line D at 39.00%. Every line is profitable, and the 38.10% aggregate falls inside their range, which is what it should do when no line is negative.
- The hidden-premium suspicion fails too. The per-unit prices differ across lines — $80.00, $50.00, $60.00, $40.00 — and different prices invite the idea of an undisclosed premium somewhere. But price times volume reproduces each line's revenue to the dollar: 550k units at $80.00 is $44,000,000, 620k at $50.00 is $31,000,000, 300k at $60.00 is $18,000,000, 175k at $40.00 is $7,000,000. The price column is redundant, not contradictory, and the 1,645k total volume adds nothing to the margin question.
- Last mile: 38.10% is confirmed and the deck needs no correction — say that in one sentence rather than hedging, because a verification that ends in "probably fine" has not been performed. Then move the conversation forward: the line margins span 35.00% to 40.00%, only 5 percentage points, so the real question is whether that 38.10% holds if the mix tilts toward Line C at 35.00%, the lowest of the four.

drills.title: Fewer, Bigger
drills.prompt: The board is alarmed: our market share fell five points in two years. How worried should they be?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Subscriber revenue bridge, FY2022 → FY2024 ($M)

lines: *Note: ARPU is a derived figure (revenue ÷ subscribers ÷ 12), rounded to the cent.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) converts the share question into dollars before answering — revenue rose from $1,260M in FY2022 to $1,470M in FY2024, +$210M or +16.67%, and subscribers rose from 8.4M to 9.2M, so the business grew while the share fell; (2) states the arithmetic cause: the denominator moved, not the numerator — the market went from $4,200M to $5,880M, +40.00%, against our +16.67%, and 1,260 / 4,200 = 30.00% while 1,470 / 5,880 = 25.00%; (3) uses percentage points for the share move — a fall of 5 percentage points, not 5% — and does not describe the share fall as a loss of customers or revenue; (4) reads the bridge as structure, not just as a total: postpaid net adds of +$168M and prepaid migration of +$84M together cover the -$84M churn drag by a factor of 3.00, so retention is not the binding problem; (5) reframes the board's concern as a growth-rate question rather than a loss question — we are growing, but the market is growing faster by a factor of 2.40 — and does not conclude that competitors are simply stronger. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that churn improved for three straight years, 18.0% to 15.1%, which contradicts any customer-loss reading; or sizes the gap by holding share flat — 30.00% of $5,880M would be $1,764M against the actual $1,470M, a shortfall of $294M.

reference.en:
- Naive: share fell from 30.0% to 25.0% in two years, so the business is shrinking and customers are walking. A five-point drop reads as an emergency, and the bridge sitting above the table reinforces it by putting a churn bar on the page.
- Correct: nothing was lost. Revenue went from $1,260M to $1,470M, a gain of $210M or +16.67%, and the subscriber count went from 8.4M to 9.2M. Both the money and the customers moved in the right direction across exactly the period the board is alarmed about.
- The share fell because the denominator moved. The market grew from $4,200M to $5,880M, +40.00%, while we grew +16.67%. Run it either way and the shares come out as stated: 1,260 / 4,200 = 30.00% and 1,470 / 5,880 = 25.00%. A ratio can fall with a rising numerator whenever the denominator rises faster, and that is the whole of what happened here.
- Say the unit correctly. Share moved 30.0% to 25.0%, which is a fall of 5 percentage points. Calling it a 5% fall names a different and far smaller event — a 5% relative decline off 30.0% would have left share at 28.5%, not 25.0%.
- The bridge answers the retention question before it is asked. Postpaid net adds contribute +$168M and prepaid migration +$84M, against a churn drag of -$84M: the two positives cover the drag by a factor of 3.00, and ARPU uplift adds a further +$42M on top. Churn is also falling year on year, 18.0% to 15.1%. Whatever is wrong, it is not that customers are leaving.
- Note what the bridge cannot show. It decomposes the change in revenue, which is the quantity that grew, while the board asked about share, which is the quantity that fell. Reading the bridge alone would leave the alarm unexplained no matter how carefully each bar is added up; the resolution only appears once the market row underneath is brought into the same sentence as our revenue row.
- Last mile: share fell 5 percentage points while revenue rose $210M, so the alarm is about a relative metric in a market that is expanding. Tell the board they are not losing the business, they are being outpaced — the market grew faster than we did by a factor of 2.40 — and hold share at 30.00% of the FY2024 market of $5,880M and we would have booked $1,764M rather than $1,470M, a gap of $294M. That is the number worth debating, and the question to take to the next meeting is whether closing it is worth what it would cost in acquisition spend and in the churn we have spent three years bringing down.

drills.title: The Last Point Turns
drills.prompt: Our supplier claims the market is in a sustained upcycle and wants a three-year commitment. What does Exhibit A tell you?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Industry revenue ($M)

lines: *Note: before 2025 the industry reported half-yearly; quarterly reporting was introduced in 2025.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) notices that the period length changes inside the series — half-years through 2024, quarters from 2025 per the note under the table — and refuses to read 590 against 1,420 as a like-for-like fall; (2) rebuilds a comparable half: 760 + 590 = 1,350 against H2 2024's 1,420, and states the move as -4.93%, so the six-period run ended rather than continued; (3) states that the deterioration accelerates inside 2025 — Q1 760 to Q2 590 is -22.37% in one quarter — and corroborates it with inventory rising 4.2 to 9.3 weeks; (4) does not treat the 61.36% climb from 880 to 1,420 as evidence of a sustained upcycle, and does not dismiss the 2025 columns as shorter-period noise without adding them back into a half; (5) converts the reading into the commitment decision: do not sign the three-year term as offered, or restructure it to a shorter term with renewal. Bonus, not required for credit: reads capacity utilisation 96 to 88 to 71 and price change +7.5 pp to -4.5 pp as two further indicators turning in the same two quarters, independently of the revenue line.

reference.en:
- Naive: six periods of unbroken growth — 880, 960, 1,040, 1,180, 1,290, 1,420 — is a climb of 61.36%, and the two 2025 bars are just the newest points on that line. Everything else in the table agreed with the supplier while the run lasted: capacity utilisation went 78% to 96% and price change went +2.0 pp to +7.5 pp over the same stretch. On that reading, locking in three years before the cycle tightens further is the prudent move.
- Correct: the last two rows are not the same length as the rows above them. The note says the industry reported half-yearly before 2025 and quarterly from 2025, so 760 and 590 are three-month figures and everything above them is six-month. Setting $590M against $1,420M sets a quarter against a half. Add the quarters back: H1 2025 = 760 + 590 = $1,350M against H2 2024 at $1,420M, which is -4.93%. The series did not continue. It broke.
- The break is the first one in the table. Every prior sequential step was positive: 880 to 960 is +9.09%, 960 to 1,040 is +8.33%, 1,040 to 1,180 is +13.46%, 1,180 to 1,290 is +9.32%, 1,290 to 1,420 is +10.08%. Six rises, then a fall — and the fall is invisible until the two quarters are combined.
- Inside 2025 the move is accelerating, not settling. Q1 760 to Q2 590 is -22.37% in a single quarter, steeper than any half-year step in the four years above it. Inventory runs the other way over exactly the same span: 4.2 weeks in H2 2024, 6.8 in Q1 2025, 9.3 in Q2 2025 — a rise by a factor of 2.21. Stock accumulating while revenue falls is the signature of a turn; a pause would show revenue softening with weeks of inventory roughly held.
- Two further indicators reverse at the same time and do not depend on the revenue arithmetic. Capacity utilisation goes 96% to 88% to 71%, and price change goes +7.5 pp to +1.0 pp to -4.5 pp — a swing of 12.0 pp that crosses from rising prices into falling prices. One series turning is a candidate for noise; three turning together inside two quarters is not.
- Last mile: the exhibit does not show a sustained upcycle, it shows an upcycle ending. On a comparable six-month basis H1 2025 at $1,350M is 4.93% below H2 2024 at $1,420M, within 2025 the fall steepens to -22.37% quarter on quarter, and inventory has reached 9.3 weeks against 4.2 two periods earlier. The three-year commitment should not be signed on this evidence: the supplier is asking to price three years off an extrapolation that the two most recent quarters already contradict. If a longer relationship is wanted, price it against the falling half rather than the rising one, or take a one-year term with renewal options and revisit once a full quarterly series exists.

drills.title: Which Way Round
drills.prompt: Operations concluded that expanding the support team causes more complaints — the two rose together every month. Do you accept that?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Support metrics, January–June 2025

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) refuses the causal claim and states why the table cannot establish it — two series rising together fix no direction between them; (2) names transactions as the third quantity moving with both, 84,000 to 216,000, +157.14% across the six months; (3) normalises the complaint count: complaints per 1,000 transactions is 5.00 in January (420 on 84,000), 5.00 in June (1,080 on 216,000) and 5.00 in every month between, so service quality is unchanged and only volume grew; (4) states the direction the other way round — complaints follow volume, hiring follows complaints, so headcount is the consequence and not the cause; (5) names a specific test that separates the explanations, such as comparing complaints per 1,000 transactions across branches whose headcount moved very differently, or finding a period where staffing moved out of proportion to volume; (6) does not treat the four columns shown as the full set of possible explanations — the boundary of the table is not the boundary of the business. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that support staff grew only 105.88%, 34 to 70, against 157.14% for complaints, so complaints per staff member rose 12.35 to 15.43, +24.90%, and hiring is lagging the load. Do not credit "correlation is not causation" without both a named alternative and a discriminating test.

reference.en:
- Naive: complaints and support staff rise together in all six months, 420 to 1,080 and 34 to 70, with no month breaking the pattern. Synchrony that clean is the most persuasive thing in the table, and headcount is the one column operations actually controls, which makes it the natural candidate for the cause. On that reading, operations should stop hiring.
- Correct: a third column moves with both. Transactions run 84,000 to 216,000, which is +157.14% over the half-year — and complaints rise by exactly the same 157.14%, 420 to 1,080. Both series grow by a factor of 2.57. Volume is carrying both, and complaints are a fixed by-product of it.
- Normalising ends the argument. Complaints per 1,000 transactions is 5.00 in January (420 on 84,000), 5.00 in June (1,080 on 216,000), and 5.00 in every month in between — not approximately, exactly. Nothing about service quality changed across the half-year. The only thing that grew is the base the complaints are drawn from.
- The claimed direction is backwards. Complaints track volume, and the support team is hired in response to the complaints, not ahead of them. Two explanations fit and both point the same way: a common driver, transaction volume, lifting complaints and headcount alike; and reverse causality, complaints pulling the hiring decision. Sample selection and a coincidence of periods do not fit — the six months are consecutive and the whole population of transactions is in the table.
- Staff is the one series that fails to keep up. Headcount goes 34 to 70, +105.88%, a factor of 2.06, against +157.14% for both complaints and transactions. Complaints per staff member therefore climb from 12.35 to 15.43, +24.90%. Hiring lags the load rather than creating it — on this evidence the team is under-resourced, and cutting the hiring plan would make the queue worse, not the complaint rate better.
- Last mile: rejecting the causal claim is one third of the answer, and on its own it is a slogan. Say why the table cannot support it: both series are being carried by transactions, up 157.14% over the same six months. Name the alternative explicitly — a common driver, volume, with reverse causality layered on top, complaints triggering the hiring. Then name the test that separates them: compare complaints per 1,000 transactions across branches whose headcount moved very differently. If the rate sits at 5.00 regardless of staffing, hiring drives complaints in neither direction; if it falls where staffing rose, hiring helps rather than harms. Without that test both stories fit the table equally well and the exhibit decides nothing.

drills.title: Same Average, New Shape
drills.prompt: Our average margin improved from 17.6% to 18.0%. The CEO wants to know if the business got healthier.

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue and margin by service line

lines: *Note: the «Share» columns and the total margin are derived from segment revenue and margin.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) compares margin segment by segment and states that all three fell — Express 28.0 to 24.0, Standard 18.0 to 16.0, Bulk 10.0 to 8.0 — with no improvement anywhere in the table; (2) attributes the rise in the average to the shift in weights and names it with numbers: Express 20.0 to 40.0% of revenue, Bulk 30.0 to 15.0% — equivalently Express $120M to $240M and Bulk $180M to $90M on an unchanged $600M total; (3) states the move as 17.60% to 18.00%, that is +0.40 percentage points, not +0.40% — reporting it as a percentage is a unit error and fails this item; (4) recognises the total margin as revenue-weighted rather than the simple average of the three segment margins, and can rebuild it: 120 x 28.0% + 300 x 18.0% + 180 x 10.0% = $105.6M on $600M, and 240 x 24.0% + 270 x 16.0% + 90 x 8.0% = $108.0M on $600M; (5) does not conclude that any segment improved — in particular, does not read the growth of Express as Express getting healthier, since its margin fell 28.0 to 24.0 — and does not accept the printed total as evidence of a healthier business; naming Express volume as the mechanism behind the mix shift is correct and must not be penalised; (6) returns the answer to what the CEO asked: the business is not healthier, and the live problem is margin erosion running across all three lines at once. Bonus, not required for credit: sizes the profit move as $105.6M to $108.0M, +2.27%; or splits the +0.40 pp into +3.20 pp of mix against -2.80 pp of margin erosion; or notes that Express lost 4.0 percentage points against 2.0 elsewhere, so the segment gaining weight is the one eroding fastest.

reference.en:
- Naive: the total line reads 17.6% in FY23 and 18.0% in FY24, up 0.40 percentage points, and the line growing fastest is the most profitable one — Express doubles from $120M to $240M and carries a 24.0% margin against the group's 18.0%. Weight moving towards the premium service while the average rises is the ordinary healthy-mix story, and the printed total appears to confirm it.
- Correct: every segment lost margin. Express 28.0 to 24.0, Standard 18.0 to 16.0, Bulk 10.0 to 8.0 — three lines out of three down, not one improvement in the table. An average that rises while all of its components fall is being moved by weights, not by performance.
- The weights did all of the work. Express share of revenue goes 20.0% to 40.0%, exactly double, and Bulk goes 30.0% to 15.0%, exactly half, so revenue shifts out of the 8.0% line and into the 24.0% line. Hold the FY23 margins of 28.0, 18.0 and 10.0 and apply the FY24 mix, and the average would have been 20.80% — the mix shift alone is worth +3.20 percentage points. Segment erosion takes back -2.80, and what survives into the total line is the +0.40 that got printed.
- Nothing actually grew. Revenue is $600M in both years, and profit moves $105.6M to $108.0M, which is +2.27%. The entire improvement the CEO is asking about is $2.4M on an unchanged top line — a rounding-scale result dressed as a margin story.
- The erosion is not even, and it is worst where the weight went. Express lost 4.0 percentage points, 28.0 to 24.0, while Standard and Bulk lost 2.0 each, 18.0 to 16.0 and 10.0 to 8.0. The segment whose share doubled is also the one whose margin fell fastest, so the line generating the mix benefit is simultaneously consuming it.
- Last mile: the business did not get healthier. Every service line is less profitable than a year ago, revenue is unchanged at $600M, and profit rose only from $105.6M to $108.0M, +2.27%, because revenue moved from Bulk at 8.0% to Express at 24.0%. The mix lever is also close to spent: Bulk is already down to 15.0% of revenue and cannot fund another shift of that size. Repeat each segment's own FY24 decline once more from the FY24 base with the mix held, and the reported average falls from 18.00% to 15.20%, profit from $108.0M to $91.2M. The question worth putting to the CEO is not what lifted the average; it is what is taking 2.0 to 4.0 percentage points a year out of every line at once — price, cost inflation or contract terms — and whether it is industry-wide, in which case the answer is repricing, or client-specific, in which case it is a book-of-business problem.

drills.title: Before What
drills.prompt: Six months after launch our new formulation shows 265,000 monthly scripts. Marketing calls the launch a failure versus the old product. Is it?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — New formulation, monthly scripts (2025)
Exhibit B — Prior formulation, quarterly scripts (2024)

lines: *Note: Exhibit A is monthly data; Exhibit B is quarterly totals.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) establishes that Exhibit A is monthly and Exhibit B is quarterly before comparing anything, and refuses to set 265,000 against 597,000 as printed; (2) converts the base to a common period, 597,000 / 3 = 199,000 prescriptions per month, and places June 2025 at 265,000 above that base by 33.17% - any answer that reports the new formulation as running below the old one fails this item; (3) brings in price as well, $61 to $84, +37.70%, and states that the revenue comparison is therefore wider than the volume comparison: June at $22.3M against a monthly-equivalent $12.1M, a factor of 1.84, and does not describe this as a doubling; (4) does not accept either false reading - that 265,000 against 597,000 shows the launch running at under half the old volume, or that Exhibit A holds no pre-launch period and so there is nothing to compare against; (5) concludes the marketing verdict is wrong and that the launch is ahead of the prior formulation on both volume and price, pointing the discussion at how fast to scale rather than at withdrawal. Bonus, not required for credit: notes the 2025 trend is +45.60% from 182,000 in March to 265,000 in June against +22.84% for the old formulation across all of 2024, so the curve is accelerating rather than flattening; notes the Revenue column is prescriptions times $84 and carries nothing the Prescriptions column does not already hold.

reference.en:
- Naive: the two headline numbers sit one exhibit apart and look made for each other. The new formulation does 265,000 scripts in June 2025; the old one did 597,000 in Q4 2024. That is under half the volume six months after launch, and the failure verdict follows without a single calculation - which is exactly why it is the wrong verdict.
- Correct: the exhibits do not run on the same clock. Exhibit A reports prescriptions by month; Exhibit B reports quarterly totals, and the note under the table says so. Q4 2024 at 597,000 scripts per quarter is 597,000 / 3 = 199,000 scripts per month. Against that base, June 2025 at 265,000 is +33.17%. The new product is ahead of the one it replaced, not at half its size.
- Price moves the same way. The old formulation sold at $61 per prescription, the new one at $84, +37.70%. Higher volume at a higher price means the revenue gap is wider than the volume gap: June revenue of $22.3M against a monthly-equivalent $12.1M for Q4 2024, which is 199,000 at $61. That is $22.3M over $12.1M, a factor of 1.84 - large, and not the doubling a quick multiplication of two increases suggests.
- The shape inside 2025 is the second argument. March 182,000 to June 265,000 is +45.60% in three months, while the old formulation needed all of 2024 to go from 486,000 to 597,000, +22.84%. The launch curve is steepening; the incumbent curve was not.
- Two parts of the tables do no work. The Revenue column is prescriptions times $84 rounded for display - 182,000 in March shows as 15.3 - so it repeats the volume column in dollars. April and May are waypoints between endpoints that already carry the trend, and Q1 and Q2 2024 play the same role in Exhibit B.
- Last mile: putting both series on a monthly basis gives a base of 199,000 prescriptions per month, and June 2025 at 265,000 clears it by 33.17% at a price 37.70% higher. Marketing has compared a month with a quarter and drawn a conclusion the data reverses. The launch beats the prior formulation on both volume and price, so the meeting should be about the rate of scale-up - supply, detailing capacity, payer coverage - and not about whether to pull the product.
