drills.title: What They Value
drills.prompt: Guest satisfaction is flat despite heavy investment. Exhibit A is what guests say matters and how they rate us; Exhibit B is where our service budget goes. Where should the next dollar go?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Guest survey, scale 1–10 (F5: attribute × dimension matrix)
Exhibit B — Service budget FY2025 ($M, F3: stack)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) builds a weighted gap instead of ranking on either survey column, importance x (10 minus rating), and says why a single column cannot set priority; (2) computes Wi-Fi reliability at 8.8 x 5.4 = 47.52 as the largest gap and check-in speed at 5.0 x 7.6 = 38.00 as the runner-up, with Wi-Fi ahead by 25.05%; (3) states that room quality, top of the importance column at 9.4, ranks only fourth on the gap at 26.32, so the correct answer matches no simple ranking; (4) reads Exhibit B against that ranking - Wi-Fi and network holds $1.1M of the $48.0M budget, 2.29%, while food holds $12.6M - and calls the allocation inverse to the priority the survey implies; (5) does not settle on either false reading as the basis of the answer: check-in speed because 2.4 is the worst rating on the page, or room quality because 9.4 is the highest importance; (6) treats the weighted gap as index points rather than as a percentage, and puts the next dollar into Wi-Fi reliability. Bonus, not required for credit: notes breakfast is the only attribute rated above its importance, 8.6 against 7.0, and carries the smallest gap at 9.80, so spend there is already past the point of return; notes gym $1.7M plus loyalty programme $1.8M is $3.5M, a factor of 3.18 more than the Wi-Fi line, which funds the reallocation without raising the $48.0M total.

reference.en:
- Naive: two single-column answers present themselves and both feel defensible. Check-in speed is rated 2.4, the worst score anywhere in the survey, so fix the worst thing. Or room quality carries importance 9.4, the highest on the page, so fund what guests care about most. Each read uses one column and throws the other away.
- Correct: priority is neither column but the product of the two - importance multiplied by the shortfall, where shortfall is 10 minus the rating. Wi-Fi reliability gives 8.8 x 5.4 = 47.52, the largest weighted gap in the survey. Check-in speed follows at 5.0 x 7.6 = 38.00, so Wi-Fi leads the field by 25.05%. The rest: loyalty programme 4.4 x 7.0 = 30.80, room quality 9.4 x 2.8 = 26.32, gym 2.6 x 6.0 = 15.60, breakfast 7.0 x 1.4 = 9.80.
- Neither obvious ranking reproduces that order. Room quality leads on importance and lands fourth on the gap at 26.32, because a 7.2 rating leaves little room to gain. Check-in speed leads on low rating and lands second at 38.00, because importance of 5.0 caps what fixing it is worth. The gap is not printed anywhere - it has to be constructed, and that is the only reason both columns are on the page.
- The gap is an index, not a percentage. 47.52 against 38.00 says Wi-Fi is the larger opportunity by 25.05% of the runner-up's size; it does not say anything is 47.52% of anything.
- Now the budget, and it runs the other way. Wi-Fi and network receives $1.1M of $48.0M, 2.29% - the smallest priority getting close to the smallest allocation is not the pattern; the largest priority getting it is. Food receives $12.6M against a breakfast gap of 9.80, the smallest in the survey. That is the flat-satisfaction-despite-investment story in one line: heavy money on the attributes with nothing left to win.
- Breakfast is the tell. It is the only attribute where the rating exceeds the importance, 8.6 against 7.0. Guests already get more of it than they ask for, so incremental breakfast spend cannot move the satisfaction number no matter how well it is executed.
- Last mile: the weighted gap puts Wi-Fi reliability at 47.52 index points against 38.00 for the next attribute, and it currently draws 2.29% of the service budget. Send the next dollar there, and fund the step change by pulling from food and the gym: gym $1.7M and loyalty programme $1.8M together are $3.5M, a factor of 3.18 more than the entire Wi-Fi and network line, and their combined importance of 2.6 plus 4.4 is 7.0, below Wi-Fi's 8.8 on its own. The reallocation moves satisfaction without moving the $48.0M total.

drills.title: Share of What Base
drills.prompt: Trelan holds 34% of the components market. What is that worth in dollars, and what does it tell you about our position?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Component supplier shares (F3: stack)
Exhibit B — Market size build-up ($B, F2: waterfall)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that Exhibit A carries shares only and that the base they are shares of is absent from it, so 34% is not yet an answer to a dollar question; (2) builds the base from Exhibit B by summing the segments, 4.20 + 1.80 + 0.60 = $6.60B, and takes the figures from the printed labels rather than from the lengths of the bars; (3) computes Trelan revenue as 34% x $6.60B = $2.244B; (4) converts the other players too - Voskild $1.782B, Marnex $1.452B, others $1.122B - and checks that the four sum back to $6.60B; (5) rejects the reading that others is negligible: at $1.122B it is 77.27% of Marnex's $1.452B and is spread over 38 plants against Marnex's 11, so it is a fragmented block the weight of the third-ranked player, not a weak one; (6) frames the competitive position in dollars rather than in share points. Bonus, not required for credit: notes the 34% headline conceals an uneven lead - transmission 19% against Marnex's 14%, but electrics 15% against Voskild's 16%; notes that plant counts and the quality index at 92, 87, 94 and 79 rank the players on other axes but offer no route to the dollar figure the question asks for.

reference.en:
- Naive: the question looks pre-answered. Trelan holds 34%, the largest block on the chart, and others at 17% is a scattered tail across 38 plants - too small and too split to be a threat. The shares are already percentages, the stack closes at 100%, and nothing about Exhibit A signals that a second exhibit is needed.
- Correct: Exhibit A has no base in it. It divides a market whose size appears only in Exhibit B, where the total is built from segments: passenger 4.20 plus commercial 1.80 plus special 0.60 = $6.60B. Take those from the labels; the bar lengths are illustration and are not drawn to a reliable scale.
- Applying the base converts every share into money. Trelan 34% x $6.60B = $2.244B. Voskild 27% = $1.782B. Marnex 22% = $1.452B. Others 17% = $1.122B. The four add back to $6.60B, which confirms the base and the shares belong to the same market.
- That conversion breaks the second false reading. Others at $1.122B is 77.27% of Marnex's $1.452B - the same order of magnitude, not a rounding line beneath it. In share points 17 against 22 reads as a distant fourth; in dollars the gap is $0.33B on a $6.60B market. And that block sits across 38 plants against Marnex's 11, so it is fragmented supply of real scale rather than one weak competitor.
- The 34% headline also hides the shape of the lead. Trelan is ahead in transmission, 19% against Marnex's 14%, but behind in electrics, 15% against Voskild's 16%. A single aggregate share averages a won sub-segment with a lost one and reports neither.
- Two columns of Exhibit A lead nowhere on this question. Plant counts have no revenue attached to them, and the quality index is dimensionless - 92, 87, 94 and 79 order the players on workmanship without pricing it. Neither can be multiplied by anything on the page.
- Last mile: the base comes from the waterfall at $6.60B, and Trelan's 34% of it is $2.244B. The position statement that follows is not the comfortable one. The fragmented tail is worth $1.122B, within reach of the named third player at $1.452B, so consolidation among those 38 plants would create a competitor of real size without a single point of share changing hands anywhere else. Assess this market in dollars, not in share points - the shares understate exactly the part of the field that can move.

drills.title: The Second Look
drills.prompt: Sales says the funnel improved at every stage this year, so the go-to-market model is working. Exhibit B is the same period. Does it change your view?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Sales funnel (F6)
Exhibit B — Demand generation (F4: dual-axis)

lines: Left axis: leads, k — from zero
Right axis: cost per lead, $ — from zero

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) confirms Exhibit A is arithmetically correct rather than disputing it — every stage rate improved, 20.00% to 22.50%, 30.00% to 35.00%, 25.00% to 28.57%, and end-to-end conversion went 900/60,000 = 1.50% to 810/36,000 = 2.25%, a gain of 0.75 percentage points; (2) states that closed-won deals still fell, 900 to 810, down 10.00%, because the funnel entrance collapsed from 60,000 to 36,000 leads, down 40.00%, so the rate gain did not offset the lost flow; (3) prices the deals in money: at an ACV of $42,000, new ARR went $37.80M to $34.02M, also down 10.00%; (4) reads Exhibit B as the second, independent problem — cost per lead $310 to $690, up 122.58%, so spend rose $18.60M to $24.84M, up 33.55%, while output fell; (5) does not accept "rates improved at every stage, so the model is working" and does not read rising spend as evidence of investing in growth; (6) points the fix at lead volume and lead cost, not at conversion, and says explicitly that Exhibit A is incomplete rather than wrong — it never shows the entrance as a variable. Bonus, not required for credit: spend per win went $18.60M/900 = about $20,667 to $24.84M/810 = about $30,667; or notes that the rate gains may themselves be a selection artefact of buying fewer, better leads.

reference.en:
- Naive: every conversion step is better in FY2024 than in FY2023 — 20.00% to 22.50% into MQL, 30.00% to 35.00% into Opportunity, 25.00% to 28.57% into closed-won. Nothing in Exhibit A is wrong, and no step got worse, so sales is reading its own chart correctly when it says the model is working.
- Correct: the funnel converts better and produces less. Closed-won went 900 to 810, down 10.00%, because the top of the funnel fell from 60,000 leads to 36,000, down 40.00%. End-to-end conversion did improve, 1.50% to 2.25% — a gain of 0.75 percentage points, a factor of 1.50 on the rate — but a 1.50x rate applied to 0.60x the volume lands at 0.90x the deals. Rates rose; output shrank.
- Exhibit A is not wrong, it is incomplete. A funnel chart shows what each stage passes to the next, and it is silent on how big the entrance is. The one number that decides the answer, 60,000 against 36,000, is the number the form is worst at making you look at.
- In money: at $42,000 per deal, new ARR went 900 x $42,000 = $37.80M to 810 x $42,000 = $34.02M, down 10.00% in step with the deals.
- Exhibit B adds the second problem, which is independent of the first. Cost per lead went $310 to $690, up 122.58%. Fewer leads at a much higher price still cost more in total: $18.60M against $24.84M, up 33.55%, or $6.24M of extra spend. First-year new ARR less demand-gen spend goes from $37.80M minus $18.60M = $19.20M to $34.02M minus $24.84M = $9.18M. Per win, $18.60M over 900 deals is about $20,667, against $24.84M over 810 deals, about $30,667.
- One reading worth holding lightly: the rate improvements may be an artefact of the same contraction. Buying 36,000 leads instead of 60,000 usually means buying the better ones first, and a cleaner intake converts better without anyone improving the selling. That would mean the funnel gains are bought, not earned — consistent with the data, though the exhibits cannot settle it.
- Last mile: sales is drawing the wrong conclusion from a correct chart. New ARR fell $37.80M to $34.02M while demand-gen spend rose $6.24M, so the go-to-market model is delivering less output for more money, and the conversion cascade is the one part that needs no repair. Fix belongs upstream: rebuild lead volume and bring cost per lead back down from $690. Ask the demand-gen team what happened to the channels that supplied the missing 24,000 leads, and whether the $690 price is mix, competition or a channel that was cut.

drills.title: The Missing Driver
drills.prompt: Marketing tripled promo spend and sales rose 52%. They want the same increase again next year. Does Exhibit A justify it?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Promo spend and sales (F4: dual-axis)

lines: Right axis: promo spend, $M — from zero

blocks.title: Exhibit B — Network and operations

lines: *Note: at the end of the previous year the network had 108 sites.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) refuses the causal claim — promo and sales rising together in Exhibit A does not establish that promo drives sales; (2) names the third quantity that sits outside Exhibit A by construction: total sites, 120 to 183, up 52.50%, against sales $84.00M to $128.10M, also up 52.50% — the same figure, not merely a similar one; (3) computes sales per site and states it is flat at $0.70M in every one of the four quarters, so no promo dollar shows up in the productivity of a site; (4) states that promo grew far faster than the network, up 195.24% from $2.10M to $6.20M against 52.50%, so promo per site rose from $2.10M/120 = $17.5k to $6.20M/183 = $33.9k, up 93.60% on the unrounded figures, with no return; (5) names the alternative explanation explicitly as a common driver — network expansion moving both series — rather than stopping at "correlation is not causation"; (6) proposes a concrete discriminating test, such as comparing sales per site within the cohort open before Q1 across different promo levels, or suspending promo in some regions and measuring the difference on comparable sites; (7) does not dismiss Exhibit B as an operations table irrelevant to a marketing question, and does not read the two-line chart as evidence of a link. Bonus, not required for credit: average ticket is flat at $24.50 across all four quarters, so neither of the two channels promo could work through moved; or that promo as a share of sales went 2.50% to 4.84%, up 2.34 percentage points.

reference.en:
- Naive: promo goes $2.10M, $3.40M, $4.80M, $6.20M and sales go $84.00M, $97.30M, $112.00M, $128.10M — up together, every quarter, no exception. A dual-axis chart puts exactly two series side by side and invites you to read the second as the consequence of the first, so asking for the same increase again looks like the obvious follow-on.
- Correct: a third quantity moves with both, and the chart cannot show it. Total sites go 120 to 183, up 52.50%. Sales go $84.00M to $128.10M, up 52.50%. Not close — the same number.
- Sales per site settles it: $84.00M/120, $97.30M/139, $112.00M/160 and $128.10M/183 are all exactly $0.70M. Four quarters, one figure. Promo nearly tripled across that span, by a factor of 2.95, and the productivity of an average site did not move by a dollar.
- The form is doing the hiding. A dual-axis chart displays two series and no more, so the site count is invisible in Exhibit A by construction. Put sites on that chart and the story collapses on sight: sales track the network, not the spend.
- The spend is getting worse per unit, not better. Promo is up 195.24% against a network up 52.50%, so promo per site went $2.10M/120 = $17.5k to $6.20M/183 = $33.9k, up 93.60%. As a share of sales, $2.10M on $84.00M is 2.50%, $6.20M on $128.10M is 4.84% — 2.34 percentage points more of revenue spent, for a flat $0.70M per site.
- Average ticket is flat at $24.50 in all four quarters, which closes the last door. Promo can work on traffic or on basket size; ticket is unchanged and sales per site is unchanged, so neither channel moved.
- Last mile: reject the causal reading — two series rising together are consistent with both being pulled by a third, and here the third is in the other exhibit. Name the alternative: a common driver, network expansion at +52.50%, exactly matching sales growth, with per-site output pinned at $0.70M. Then name the test that separates the stories: compare sales per site inside the cohort of locations already open before Q1, across quarters with different promo levels, or hold promo flat in a set of regions and measure the gap against comparable sites. Note also what the request actually asks for: repeating the increase from the Q4 run rate of $6.20M, not from $2.10M, means about $18.30M a quarter, and nothing in these exhibits says the first $6.20M bought anything.

drills.title: Say It Plainly
drills.prompt: The board deck claims a 28.9% contribution margin. Verify it and state plainly whether the claim stands.

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Contribution by product line ($M)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) verifies the headline directly — ($200.0M minus $142.2M)/$200.0M = 28.90% — and states plainly that the claim stands; (2) checks that the line items sum to the stated totals: 86.0 + 44.0 + 52.0 + 18.0 = 200.0 and 61.06 + 30.80 + 39.00 + 11.34 = 142.2, so there is no hidden line and no unallocated cost; (3) checks volume x price against revenue on every line, 1,075k t x $80.00 = $86.0M, 2,200k t x $20.00 = $44.0M, 650k t x $80.00 = $52.0M, 60k t x $300.00 = $18.0M, all four exact; (4) checks that no line is loss-making — 29.00%, 30.00%, 25.00%, 37.00%, all positive; (5) states explicitly that there is no trap here and says why: no negative line, no price inconsistent with revenue, no rebasing needed, one period and one base. Saying only "28.90% is correct" without naming the absence of a trap does not earn this item; (6) does not manufacture a distortion out of the Additives price of $300.00/t against $20.00/t for Aggregates, and does not assert an unprofitable line dragging the aggregate. Bonus, not required for credit: the mix-weighted check, with shares taken as 86.0/200.0 = 43.00%, 44.0/200.0 = 22.00%, 52.0/200.0 = 26.00% and 18.0/200.0 = 9.00%, giving 43.00% x 29.00 + 22.00% x 30.00 + 26.00% x 25.00 + 9.00% x 37.00 = 28.90; or flagging that Concrete carries the lowest margin at 25.00% on the second-largest revenue of $52.0M as the mix question to ask next.

reference.en:
- Naive: the instinct is to hunt. Additives sell at $300.00/t against $20.00/t for Aggregates, fifteen times the price on the same tonnage basis, so a hidden premium must be inflating the blend; or one line must be losing money and quietly dragging the total. Both suspicions are reasonable to form and both are wrong here, and the work is to say so rather than to keep digging.
- Correct: the claim verifies. Contribution is $200.0M minus $142.2M = $57.8M, and $57.8M/$200.0M = 28.90%. That is the number in the deck, to the decimal.
- The totals are real, not asserted. Revenue lines sum to 86.0 + 44.0 + 52.0 + 18.0 = 200.0 and variable costs to 61.06 + 30.80 + 39.00 + 11.34 = 142.2. Nothing sits outside the four lines, so there is no unallocated cost bucket where a surprise could hide.
- The price premium is real and harmless. Volume x price reproduces stated revenue exactly on all four lines: 1,075 x $80.00 = $86.0M, 2,200 x $20.00 = $44.0M, 650 x $80.00 = $52.0M, 60 x $300.00 = $18.0M. Additives really do sell at fifteen times the Aggregates price, and that premium is already inside the $200.0M — it distorts nothing, because the margin is computed on the same revenue the prices produce.
- No line is loss-making. Cement contributes $86.0M minus $61.06M = $24.94M, 29.00%; Aggregates $13.20M, 30.00%; Concrete $13.00M, 25.00%; Additives $6.66M, 37.00%. All four positive, and the four contributions sum to $57.8M.
- A third route lands in the same place. Weight each line margin by that line's share of the $200.0M: Cement 86.0/200.0 = 43.00% at 29.00%, Aggregates 44.0/200.0 = 22.00% at 30.00%, Concrete 52.0/200.0 = 26.00% at 25.00%, Additives 18.0/200.0 = 9.00% at 37.00%. The four products sum to 12.47 + 6.60 + 6.50 + 3.33 = 28.90%. Three independent checks, one answer.
- Last mile: the claim is correct and needs no qualification, and the useful skill here is saying that without hedging. There is no trap: no negative line, no price that fails to reconcile with revenue, no rebasing, one period and one base, and the suspicions worth forming were formed and dismissed on the numbers rather than waved off. What is worth raising next is not a correction but a question: the spread runs 25.00% to 37.00%, twelve percentage points wide, and the lowest-margin line, Concrete at 25.00%, carries the second-largest revenue at $52.0M — so ask how stable 28.90% is if the mix keeps tilting toward Concrete.

drills.title: Parallel Lines
drills.prompt: Our CEO points at the chart: "Both lines are parallel — we're keeping pace with the leader." Is that the right read?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Annual revenue, log scale ($M)

lines: Right axis: market share, % — linear, from zero

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) identifies the left axis as logarithmic and states what parallel means on it — equal growth rate, not equal distance — with the gridlines 400 / 800 / 1,600 / 3,200 / 6,400 as the evidence, since equal spacing there carries a constant doubling rather than a constant increment; (2) confirms both series do grow at the same rate, a factor of 1.5 in every step, 400 to 2,025 and 1,200 to 6,075 across four steps, which compounds to 50.00% a year, and does not claim either company is growing faster than the other; (3) computes the dollar gap at both ends — 1,200 minus 400 = $800M in 2020 and 6,075 minus 2,025 = $4,050M in 2024 — and states it widened by a factor of 5.0625; (4) reads the flat market share as confirmation rather than as a separate fact: 8.0% in all five years means Verrindale's position has not moved while its revenue multiplied by 5.0625; (5) rejects "the lines are parallel, so the deficit is not growing" and does not accept that one shared axis makes the comparison direct — the axis is shared and still misleads, because it is logarithmic; (6) concludes that matching the leader's rate can never close the gap and that catching up requires a rate above 50.00% a year. Bonus, not required for credit: notes the ratio is 3.000 in every year, which fixes the gap at a factor of 2.000 on Verrindale's revenue and forces it to compound at the same 50.00%; or projects one more year at the same pace — $3,037.5M against $9,112.5M, a gap of $6,075M, widening by $2,025M in twelve months.

reference.en:
- Naive: the two lines run parallel across all five years, on one axis, with the ratio column holding at 3.000 in 2020 and 3.000 in 2024. Nothing in the picture moves apart, so nothing in the business is moving apart either — Verrindale is keeping pace, exactly as the CEO says.
- Correct: the left axis is logarithmic. Its gridlines are 400, 800, 1,600, 3,200 and 6,400 — each one twice the last, printed at equal spacing. Equal spacing on that axis therefore means equal ratio, not equal difference. Two parallel lines mean two identical growth rates, and identical rates on unequal bases push the money gap wider every year. Verrindale runs 400 to 2,025 and the leader 1,200 to 6,075, each step a factor of 1.5, four steps, which is 50.00% a year for both.
- The dollars are where parallel stops being reassuring. In 2020 the gap is 1,200 minus 400 = $800M; in 2024 it is 6,075 minus 2,025 = $4,050M. That is a factor of 5.0625, and $3,250M of ground surrendered while the chart showed two lines holding formation.
- The gap is not an independent quantity, which is why it had no choice. The leader is 3.000 times Verrindale in every year, so the gap is exactly twice Verrindale's revenue: 2 times 400 = 800, and 2 times 2,025 = 4,050. A constant ratio forces the gap to compound at whatever rate the revenue compounds at, so the gap grows by 5.0625 because the revenue grew by 5.0625. It is the same number twice.
- Market share says it again without arithmetic: 8.0% in 2020 and 8.0% in 2024, flat for five straight years. Revenue multiplied by 5.0625 and the position did not move at all, which is what growing at exactly the market rate looks like. The implied market follows from the same two columns — 400 divided by 0.080 = $5,000M in 2020 against 2,025 divided by 0.080 = $25,312.5M in 2024 — the same factor of 5.0625 once more.
- Price the next twelve months at the CEO's own assumption. Hold both rates and Verrindale books 2,025 times 1.5 = $3,037.5M against the leader's 6,075 times 1.5 = $9,112.5M, a gap of $6,075M. The deficit widens by $2,025M in one year — the whole of Verrindale's current annual revenue added to the shortfall, while the two lines stay exactly as parallel as they are now.
- Last mile: parallel means equal rate, not equal distance, so the read inverts the chart. The absolute gap went $800M to $4,050M, a factor of 5.0625, while share sat at 8.0% for five years — keeping pace is what locks the deficit in, not what closes it. Tell the CEO that holding 50.00% guarantees the gap keeps compounding, and that any catch-up plan has to clear the leader's rate rather than match it. Two things to bring back: where a rate above 50.00% could come from, meaning segments the leader does not hold or price and attach on the existing base; and this same data redrawn on a linear axis, where the divergence is visible without anyone having to do the arithmetic.

drills.title: Last One Standing
drills.prompt: Our share went from 12% to 19% in three years. The board calls it a turnaround. Do you agree?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Our revenue bridge, FY2021 → FY2024 ($M)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) converts the share move into dollars before judging it — revenue fell from $288M to $228M, down $60M or 20.83%, across the same three years the board is celebrating; (2) states the arithmetic cause: the market fell from $2,400M to $1,200M, down 50.00%, so 288 / 2,400 = 12.00% and 228 / 1,200 = 19.00% — the denominator fell faster than the numerator; (3) uses percentage points for the share move, a rise of 7 percentage points, and does not call it a 7% rise or describe it as revenue gained; (4) reads the bridge as the mechanism rather than as a total, naming the +$96M inflow from exited competitors as revenue that arrived rather than revenue that was won, setting it against the -$132M fall in demand, and checking that the four drivers net to +96 - 132 + 24 - 48 = -$60M; (5) rejects "share is up, so we are growing" and does not treat 19.0% alongside 11 publishers as evidence of market leadership — the exhibit gives no other publisher's share; (6) concludes this is not a turnaround and frames the decision as whether to stay in a market that halved, not how to defend the 19.0%. Bonus, not required for credit: prices the genuine part of the outperformance — at a flat 12.00% share FY2024 revenue would be 12.00% of $1,200M = $144M against the actual $228M, so $84M of it is real relative gain; or notes the +$24M price increase is half the size of the -$48M subscriber churn, so the price lever is already netting negative.

reference.en:
- Naive: share went from 12.0% to 19.0% in three years, a rise of 7 percentage points, and the field thinned from 34 publishers to 11. Halwick is one of the survivors and now a much larger fish, so the board's word for it is turnaround.
- Correct: the fish grew because the pond drained faster. Revenue fell from $288M to $228M, down $60M or 20.83%, over exactly the three years being celebrated. The market fell from $2,400M to $1,200M, down 50.00%. Share is the ratio of those two lines, and a ratio rises whenever the denominator falls faster than the numerator: 288 / 2,400 = 12.00% and 228 / 1,200 = 19.00%. Nothing in those 7 percentage points required Halwick to sell more of anything.
- The bridge names the mechanism in one bar. Of the moves from FY2021 to FY2024, +$96M is inflow from exited competitors — revenue that landed because 23 of the 34 publishers stopped printing, not because Halwick took it from anyone. Against it sits -$132M of falling demand, the largest driver on the page, and those two alone net to -$36M. Add the rest and the four drivers give +96 - 132 + 24 - 48 = -$60M, which is the whole of the change.
- Strip out the inheritance and the underlying business reads worse than the headline: $228M less the $96M of inflow is $132M against a FY2021 base of $288M, a fall of 54.17%. The departed competitors handed over most of what the demand collapse took away, and the board is reading that handover as performance.
- Give the share gain the credit it is owed, then price it. Had share stayed at 12.00%, FY2024 revenue would have been 12.00% of $1,200M = $144M; Halwick booked $228M, so $84M of the outcome is genuine outperformance against a collapsing market. That is worth something and it is not a turnaround. Over the same window the market lost $1,200M and Halwick lost $60M — a factor of 20.00, which is the whole reason the ratio moved in our favour.
- Price is already pulling the wrong way. The +$24M from the price increase stands against -$48M of subscriber churn, exactly half its size: the increase brought in less revenue than the subscribers it cost. That is a lever near the end of its travel, not one with room left in it.
- Last mile: revenue fell $60M, or 20.83%, while share rose 7 percentage points, so the share gain is arithmetic rather than achievement — the market halved and the +$96M came from 23 departed publishers. Tell the board this is consolidation of a market that is disappearing, not a recovery. Run the same three years again and the $1,200M market halves to $600M, the $228M falls another 20.83% to $180.5M, and share climbs to 30.08% while the business shrinks by a further fifth — the metric they are cheering improves fastest in the scenario they should fear most. The question for the next meeting is not how to defend 19.0%; it is whether print stays in the portfolio, and the number that answers it is the standalone economics of $228M of revenue in a $600M market.

drills.title: Revenue Is Not Profit
drills.prompt: Which channel is most profitable? Management wants to double down on the biggest one.

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Revenue by channel, FY2024 ($M, stack)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that the question asks about profit while the exhibit carries only revenue, and names what is absent — no margin, no cost of goods, no cost-to-serve, no channel P&L; (2) concludes the question cannot be answered as posed on this data, rather than nominating a channel anyway; (3) rejects "Retail is the largest at $420M and 46.7%, so it is the most profitable" — size is not profitability; (4) rejects the completeness illusion of the stack: splitting Retail into $270M and $150M and Wholesale into $190M and $90M adds resolution on revenue only, and every level of the stack is the same variable; (5) uses the customer counts as a direction to test rather than as an answer — Retail's $420M spread over 2,140 customers against Wholesale's $280M over 96, roughly $196,262 versus roughly $2,916,667 per account — and marks the cost-to-serve implication as untested, since the exhibit prices no cost at all; (6) names the data to request, contribution margin or cost-to-serve by channel, as the step that has to precede any doubling down. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that Direct grows +19% a year against Retail's +3% and that growth is a third variable answering neither question; or notes Retail carries 22.29 times the customers of Wholesale for 1.5 times the revenue.

reference.en:
- Naive: the stack goes all the way down. $900M splits into four channels, and two of those split again into named sub-channels, so the picture looks finished. Retail is the largest at $420M, 46.7% of the total, and doubling down on Retail is doubling down on the biggest thing on the page.
- Correct: the question is about profit and the exhibit contains no cost of any kind. There is no margin column, no cost of goods, no cost-to-serve, no channel P&L. What the page ranks is revenue — Retail $420M, Wholesale $280M, Direct $120M, Export $80M, summing to $900M — and that ranking is silent on profit, because profit is revenue less a quantity nobody printed.
- Depth is not completeness. Breaking Retail into $270M of chain stores and $150M of independents, and Wholesale into $190M and $90M, adds resolution along the axis that was already there. Each level of the stack is the same variable measured more finely. An exhibit can be arbitrarily detailed on revenue and be no closer to a profit answer than a single total would be.
- The one column that does hint at something points away from the naive read. Retail's $420M is spread across 2,140 customers, roughly $196,262 each, while Wholesale's $280M sits with 96 customers, roughly $2,916,667 each — 22.29 times the accounts for 1.5 times the revenue, a factor of 14.86 in revenue per account. Serving 2,140 relationships plausibly costs more than serving 96: coverage, delivery drops, receivables, returns.
- Hold that lightly, because it is exactly what the exhibit cannot settle. Retail may carry a gross margin wide enough to pay for all of that overhead and more; a channel with 96 accounts may be 96 accounts with all the negotiating power. Both readings survive this data unscathed, and that is the diagnosis rather than a tie — the exhibit does not discriminate between them, so no amount of care in reading it will.
- Growth is a third variable aimed at neither question. Direct compounds at +19% a year against Retail's +3%, and it is the second smallest channel at $120M. Fast growth is not profit either, and a $120M channel at +19% cannot be ranked against a $420M channel at +3% without the same costs that are missing everywhere else.
- Last mile: the question is about profit, the data is about revenue, and it cannot be answered as posed. The missing quantity is contribution margin or cost-to-serve by channel — one column beside the four revenue lines and the ranking resolves in a sentence. Do not double down on Retail on the strength of $420M and 46.7% of the mix; that is a size argument wearing a profit label, and it is the specific mistake this chart invites. First step is to request a channel-level P&L with cost-to-serve allocated on the driver that actually separates these channels, the 2,140 Retail accounts against 96 in Wholesale, and to decide where the next dollar goes only once that column exists.

drills.title: Every Winter
drills.prompt: The CFO is worried: Q4 revenue is half of Q2. Is there a problem with the business?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Quarterly revenue ($M)

lines: *Note: garden centres are a seasonal business; the peak falls in the planting season (April–June) and the trough in the winter months.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) compares each quarter with the same quarter of the prior year instead of with a neighbouring quarter, and states that all four moves are positive, +9.7%, +10.2%, +10.4%, +11.1%, with the full year up from $330M to $364M, +10.3%; (2) names the sign flip out loud — four cells carry both readings, 60/130 - 1 = -53.85% down the 2024 column and 60/54 - 1 = +11.11% across the Q4 row — and says which of the two answers the CFO's question; (3) rejects the reversal reading with evidence rather than assertion: the curve repeats, Q2 is the peak and Q4 the trough in 2023 and again in 2024, and every quarter of 2024 sits above its 2023 counterpart; (4) rejects the volatility reading by showing the swing is stable rather than growing — 118/54 = 2.19 in 2023 against 130/60 = 2.17 in 2024, so the amplitude is a property of the market, not a sign of instability; (5) states explicitly that there is no problem to find, rather than hedging or manufacturing one, and names the error as comparing quarters against each other in a business whose quarters are not comparable; (6) does not treat the footnote as the proof — the note asserts seasonality, the two-year comparison is what demonstrates it. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that the growth rate accelerates through the year, +9.7% in Q1 to +11.1% in Q4; or that the fastest-growing quarter is the smallest one, so Q2 still carries $12M of the $34M the year gained while Q4 carries $6M.

reference.en:
- Naive: inside 2024 the business runs 130 in Q2 down to 60 in Q4: 60/130 - 1 = -53.85%, and it did the same thing the year before, 118 down to 54. Losing more than half of quarterly revenue between spring and winter, twice in a row, looks like a business coming apart, and the CFO is asking the obvious question.
- Correct: the comparison is drawn along the wrong axis. Q4 is not the successor of Q2 in any economic sense — it is the successor of the previous Q4. Set Q4 against Q4 and revenue went 54 to 60, +11.1%. The other three do the same: Q1 62 to 68, +9.7%, Q2 118 to 130, +10.2%, Q3 96 to 106, +10.4%. The year went $330M to $364M, +10.3%. Nothing in the table is negative once it is read across rather than down.
- The sign flip is the whole exercise. Four cells carry it. Read down the 2024 column, Q2 130 to Q4 60: 60/130 - 1 = -53.85%. Read across the Q4 row, 2023 54 to 2024 60: 60/54 - 1 = +11.11%. Both are arithmetically correct; only one of them is about the business. What decides between them is not in the numbers — it is that a garden centre sells plants in the planting season and does not sell them in December.
- Regularity is what separates seasonality from a trend, and it is measurable here rather than assumed. Q2 over Q4 is 118/54 = 2.19 in 2023 and 130/60 = 2.17 in 2024. Q2 takes 118 of 330 and then 130 of 364 — 35.76% and 35.71% of the year. A business that was actually turning over would not reproduce its own curve to within a tenth of a percentage point.
- Take the footnote as a claim, not as the answer. It says the business is seasonal and the trough falls in winter; a candidate who only quotes it has verified nothing. The two-year comparison is what proves the claim, and it would have exposed the note as wrong if 2024 had broken the pattern.
- The one real observation runs the other way: growth accelerates through the year, +9.7% in Q1 to +11.1% in Q4. Note what that is worth in money before calling it a finding — the fastest-growing quarter is the smallest, so Q4 adds $6M while Q2 at the slower +10.2% adds $12M of the $34M gained (130 against 118, 364 against 330).
- Last mile: the swing is regular, the amplitude is unchanged, and every quarter grew, so the year rose from $330M to $364M and the CFO's concern is not supported by the exhibit. Say so directly: no restatement, no corrective action, and no quarter-on-quarter comparison in a seasonal business. The question worth taking forward is not why Q4 is small but why the growth rate climbs from +9.7% to +11.1% across the year — whether that is price, footfall or a mix shift into the winter range.

drills.title: Tonnes and Units
drills.prompt: Our largest product by volume is fasteners — 42 million units. Should it get priority in the capacity plan?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Product portfolio, FY2024

lines: *Note: no «total volume» row is given — tonnes and units do not add up.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) states that tonnes and units are physically different quantities with no conversion between them, so the Volume column cannot be ranked as one column, and does not attempt to convert 42,000,000 units into tonnes or the reverse; (2) names money as the only base shared by all four rows and ranks on it: fasteners 42,000,000 x $0.85 = $35.70M, 6.8% of revenue and last of the four, against rolled steel 480,000 x $620.00 = $297.60M, 57.1% and first — a factor of 8.34; (3) explains the gap through price rather than through error, $0.85 per unit against $620.00 per tonne; (4) answers the capacity question against fasteners — 6.8% of $521.20M does not earn priority — and names rolled steel as the product that does; (5) does not accept that the four numbers are comparable because they sit under one heading, and does not carry the volume ranking across into an expectation about revenue share. Bonus, not required for credit: totals only what can be totalled, 480,000 + 120,000 + 95,000 = 695,000 t carrying $485.50M of the $521.20M; or reads pipe against rolled steel, 120,000 t against 480,000 t earning $117.60M against $297.60M, and concludes that price per tonne matters as much as tonnage even among the comparable rows.

reference.en:
- Naive: the Volume column carries one heading and four numbers, and 42,000,000 is the largest of them — 42,000,000/480,000 = 87.5 times rolled steel. Largest product by volume, therefore first claim on capacity. The table appears to have answered the question before it was asked.
- Correct: that column is not a column. Three rows are in tonnes and one is in units, and no coefficient converts between them — a tonne measures mass, a unit counts objects. 42,000,000 fasteners and 480,000 tonnes of rolled steel are not two values of one quantity, so neither is larger than the other. The exhibit gives no total volume, and it cannot: the addition is undefined.
- The only base all four rows share is money. Fasteners: 42,000,000 x $0.85 = $35.70M, and $35.70M against $521.20M is 6.85% of revenue. Rolled steel: 480,000 x $620.00 = $297.60M, 57.1%. On the one axis that ranks all four, the order is rolled steel $297.60M, pipe $117.60M, sections $70.30M, fasteners $35.70M. Fasteners are last, not first, and 297.60/35.70 = 8.34 says by how much.
- Price is why, and it is printed. $620.00 a tonne against $0.85 a unit is a ratio of 729.4. A product priced under a dollar has to sell in the tens of millions before it shows up next to one priced in the hundreds, which is exactly what the volume figure records — a consequence of the price, not a measure of importance.
- What can be added, add. The three tonnage rows total 480,000 + 120,000 + 95,000 = 695,000 t, and they carry $297.60M + $117.60M + $70.30M = $485.50M of the $521.20M, 93.15%. Fasteners are the single row that sits outside that arithmetic, and they are also the single row that cannot be argued for on the same terms as the others.
- Worth one more line while the money is on the table. Pipe runs 120,000 t against rolled steel's 480,000 t — a quarter of the tonnage — and earns $117.60M against $297.60M, 39.52% of the revenue, because it prices at $980.00 a tonne against $620.00. Even among the rows that are comparable, tonnage alone ranks them wrongly.
- Last mile: volumes across the four rows do not compare, revenue does, and on revenue fasteners are $35.70M of $521.20M, 6.8%, against rolled steel at $297.60M, 57.1% — so capacity priority goes to rolled steel. Withdraw the premise before arguing the plan: "largest by volume" compares two quantities that have no common scale, and any capacity case built on it inherits the error. The next number to ask for is contribution margin per tonne of capacity, since revenue share still says nothing about what a tonne of capacity earns.

drills.title: Biggest Is Not Best
drills.prompt: We can enter one segment next year. Which one, and what's the size of the opportunity?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Segment matrix

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) rejects market size as the selection axis and gives the reason from the data — Cardiology is already 65% ours, so only 35% of $180M, or $63M, is available, against 85% of $100M, or $85M, in Surgical; (2) computes headroom for all four segments as size x (1 - penetration) x (1 + growth): Cardiology $65.5M, Imaging $71.3M, Surgical $103.7M, Dental $60.0M; (3) names Surgical as the answer at $103.7M against the next best $71.3M, a gap of $32.4M, and states that it is neither the largest segment, third of four by size, nor the fastest growing, second at 22%; (4) states that the three available axes give three different answers — size picks Cardiology, growth picks Dental, unoccupied market picks Surgical — and that Dental, fastest at 25% a year, still finishes last at $60.0M; (5) does not read the Our revenue column as opportunity: Cardiology's $117.0M is the largest part of our $198.0M and measures the position we already hold, not what is left to take. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that Surgical leads before growth is applied at all, $85M of unoccupied market against Imaging's $66M; or treats Surgical's 12 distributors against Cardiology's 41 as a cost-of-entry question that does not change which segment is largest.

reference.en:
- Naive: Cardiology is the biggest number on the page, $180M of a $460M market, so that is where the opportunity is. The second version of the same mistake picks Dental for growing 25% a year. Both take one column as decisive and stop there.
- Correct: the question is which segment to enter, and what can be entered is the part of the market not already held. Penetration turns the ranking over. Cardiology is 65% ours, which leaves 35% of it free: 180 x 0.35 = $63M is open. Surgical is 15% ours, which leaves 85% free: 100 x 0.85 = $85M is open. The largest segment on the page offers the third-largest opening of four.
- Carry it forward a year and the order holds. Headroom = size x (1 - penetration) x (1 + growth): Cardiology 180 x 0.35 x 1.04 = $65.5M, Imaging 120 x 0.55 x 1.08 = $71.3M, Surgical 100 x 0.85 x 1.22 = $103.7M, Dental 60 x 0.80 x 1.25 = $60.0M. Surgical takes it by $32.4M over Imaging; measured against Imaging's unrounded 120 x 0.55 x 1.08 = 71.28, Surgical is 45.48% larger.
- Growth is not what wins it. Before any growth multiplier is applied, Surgical already leads on unoccupied market, $85M against Imaging's $66M, 28.79% ahead. Growth widens the gap; it does not create it. And Dental proves growth cannot be trusted alone: the fastest rate in the matrix, 25%, finishes last at $60.0M, because a high rate on the smallest base and the smallest opening on the page is still the smallest number on the page.
- Three columns, three answers — which is the point of the matrix. Size says Cardiology, growth says Dental, unoccupied market says Surgical. Only the third one is aligned with the question that was asked, and nothing in the layout marks it out; the column that decides sits fourth, after the two that mislead.
- The Our revenue column is the mirror of the trap. Cardiology contributes $117.0M of our $198.0M, so it is comfortably our largest business, and that is a statement about where we already are. Penetration and our revenue are the same fact written twice — 180 x 0.65 = 117.0 — and a segment where both are high is by construction a segment with little left in it.
- The one real argument against: Surgical carries 12 distributors against Cardiology's 41 and Dental's 34, so entering it means building the channel where ours is thinnest. That is a cost and timing question. It changes what capturing $103.7M would cost; it does not change that $103.7M is the largest opening available.
- Last mile: ranked by what is actually free rather than by what is large, Surgical is the entry at $103.7M of addressable headroom against $71.3M for the next best, so enter Surgical. Cardiology cannot be the answer at 65% penetration no matter how large it looks — the arithmetic caps it at $65.5M. Next step is to price the channel: what it costs and how long it takes to go from 12 distributors to coverage, and whether that spend still leaves Surgical ahead of Imaging's $71.3M on a net basis.

drills.title: The Row That Doesn't Matter
drills.prompt: Is the underwriting business profitable? One row here is irrelevant to that question — which, and why?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Insurance results, FY2024

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) names the combined ratio as the measure of underwriting profitability and computes it from the exhibit, ($546M + $168M) / $840M = 85.00%, reading below 100% as profitable with 15.00 percentage points of headroom; (2) identifies investment income, $63M, as the row irrelevant to the question AND gives the reason as its nature rather than its size: it is an investing result, not an underwriting one, and the combined ratio excludes it by definition; (3) keeps the policy count and the average premium as relevant rather than striking them, because 420 thousand x $2,000 = $840M reconciles the premiums row, so those two rows verify the input the whole ratio rests on; (4) does not accept "investment income is irrelevant because it is the smallest number, $63M" as a sufficient answer, and does not accept that every printed row must be needed. Bonus, not required for credit: splits the ratio into claims $546M / $840M = 65.00% and expenses $168M / $840M = 20.00%; or prices the exclusion, underwriting profit is $840M - $546M - $168M = $126M against $63M of investment income, so folding the two together would let a combined ratio above 100% still print a positive total.

reference.en:
- Naive: six rows are printed and the smallest of them is investment income at $63M, so if one row has to go it is that one, since it barely moves anything. Or, from the other side: every row in an exhibit was put there for a reason, so nothing on the page is truly irrelevant.
- Correct: underwriting profitability is measured by the combined ratio, claims plus expenses over premiums: ($546M + $168M) / $840M = 85.00%. Anything below 100% means the insurance business earns money on the policies themselves, and 85.00% clears that line by 15.00 percentage points.
- The irrelevant row is investment income, and the reason has nothing to do with how small it is. Investment income is the return earned on the float, an investing result; the combined ratio measures the underwriting result. The row is excluded by the definition of the metric.
- Test that reasoning by reversing it. Had investment income been the largest number on the page it would still be excluded, and had claims been the smallest they would still sit inside the ratio. Size decides nothing here; the definition of the metric decides everything. Pointing at the right row for the wrong reason is not the same answer.
- The two rows that never enter the calculation are still relevant. Policies, 420 thousand, times average premium, $2,000, gives $840,000,000, which is exactly the premiums row. A row that reconciles the data is doing work even when it appears in no formula: it is the reason to trust the $840M that everything else divides by.
- Breaking the ratio into its parts, claims are $546M / $840M = 65.00% of premiums and operating expenses are $168M / $840M = 20.00%. Claims dominate the cost structure, so that is where a combined ratio moves from.
- In money: $840M - $546M - $168M = $126M of underwriting profit, and investment income of $63M would sit on top for $189M pre-tax. Note the sizes: investment income of $63M against the $840M - $546M - $168M = $126M earned on the policies, exactly half. That is the reason the two results are reported apart rather than netted: an investing line of that weight can carry an underwriting line that has stopped working.
- What the separation protects against is not visible in this year's numbers, which is the point of the discipline. Claims would have to rise from $546M to $672M, premiums of $840M less expenses of $168M, before underwriting broke even. Only past that point does the merged total start telling a story the insurance business does not support.
- Last mile: the combined ratio is 85.00%, so underwriting is profitable with 15.00 percentage points of headroom, and the row to strike from the answer is investment income at $63M, not because it is the smallest figure on the page but because it measures a different business. Keep the policy count and the average premium: 420 thousand x $2,000 = $840M is the check that the premium line is real. The next question to put to the client is whether the claims ratio of $546M / $840M = 65.00% holds across the whole book or is being carried by one segment, because that is the ratio with the room to move.

drills.title: Depends What You Ask
drills.prompt: Two sources give different 2024 sales. Finance wants to know which one is reliable so we can standardise on it. What do you tell them?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — POS (own tills), $M

lines: *Note: POS records every receipt in the chain's own stores. Own outlets account for **90%** of all brand sales; the rest goes through marketplaces and partner retail.*

blocks.title: Exhibit B — Consumer panel, $M (annual estimates)

rows: Share of wallet in the category, %

lines: *Note: the panel is built on a sample of 12,000 households and extrapolated to the population; it captures purchases across all channels, but the volume is an estimate.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) works from the two footnotes rather than the totals alone, since the 90% coverage note is what resolves the case; re-adding the POS quarters is neither required nor penalised, the year total of $1,242M is printed in bold; (2) explains the $138M difference by coverage rather than by error: own outlets are 90% of brand sales, $1,242M / 0.90 = $1,380M matches the panel total exactly, and $138M of $1,380M is 10.00%, the sales made through marketplaces and partner retail; (3) states that neither source contains an error, POS being exact within its scope while the panel's volume is an estimate extrapolated from a sample of 12,000 households; (4) rejects the premise that one source is reliable in general and assigns sources by question instead: own-store revenue to POS at $1,242M, while share of wallet and buyer age mix can only come from the panel, the only exhibit carrying those rows; (5) declines to standardise on a single source and does not answer with a winner; (6) does not accept "POS is quarterly and receipt-level, therefore more accurate", since detail inside a 90% scope does not extend the scope. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that the 35-54 segment fell $542M to $524M, -3.32%, while the panel total rose $1,290M to $1,380M, +6.98%, a movement invisible in POS at any granularity; or checks that the panel segments sum to their totals, 387 + 542 + 361 = 1,290 and 456 + 524 + 400 = 1,380.

reference.en:
- Naive: two systems report two different numbers for the same year, $1,242M and $1,380M, so one of them must be wrong and the task is to find out which. POS looks like the winner on sight: it records every receipt, it is broken out by quarter, and it is the chain's own system, while the panel is 12,000 households scaled up to a whole population.
- Correct: the two numbers do not contradict each other, because they do not measure the same thing. Take the POS year as printed, $1,242M, and go straight to the footnote: own outlets are 90% of all brand sales. $1,242M / 0.90 = $1,380M, which is the panel total exactly. The $138M difference is not error, it is the marketplace and partner-retail volume that no till in the chain ever sees. As a share, $138M of $1,380M is 10.00%, the complement of the 90% coverage, as it has to be.
- Neither source is wrong, and neither is reliable in general. POS is exact within its scope and finer in time. The panel is broader in scope and is the only place where buyer segments and share of wallet exist at all, but its volume is an estimate extrapolated from a sample of 12,000 households.
- Granularity is not accuracy, and the quarters are the trap on this page. They are the most detailed thing in either exhibit and the least load-bearing: 284, 301, 318 and 339 add to the $1,242M already printed in bold and say nothing about the sales the source cannot observe. Re-deriving a total that is given buys nothing; the sentence that decides the case is the footnote underneath it. A precise measurement of the wrong scope stays wrong however finely it is cut.
- So the question as Finance framed it has no answer, and the answer belongs to the question underneath it. How much did we sell in our own stores goes to POS, $1,242M. What share of the category do we hold, and who is buying, goes to the panel and nowhere else: share of wallet moved 14.2% to 15.1%, up 0.9 percentage points, and the age split sits only in Exhibit B.
- One row is enough to show what standardising would cost. Panel brand sales rose $1,290M to $1,380M, +$90M or +6.98%, and inside that total the 35-54 buyers fell $542M to $524M, -$18M or -3.32%, while 18-34 rose $387M to $456M, +$69M or +17.83% and 55+ rose $361M to $400M, +$39M or +10.80%. Growth is coming from both ends of the age range while the middle contracts. The segments reconcile to their totals in both years, 387 + 542 + 361 = 1,290 and 456 + 524 + 400 = 1,380, so this is the panel's own arithmetic and not an artefact of the extrapolation.
- The instinct behind the request is still worth honouring. Two totals for one year in two decks is a real reporting problem; the fix is a stated scope on each number, not the deletion of one of them.
- Last mile: both sources are correct, the gap is $138M of $1,380M, the sales made outside our own outlets, and standardising on one of them would delete a question rather than answer it. Assign by question instead: POS is the book of record for own-store revenue at $1,242M, the panel is the book of record for market share and buyer mix at $1,380M, and every report states which scope it is on. The first action is to write that mapping down and stop presenting the two totals as rival estimates of one quantity. The second is to put an owner on the $138M itself, because $138M of $1,380M currently exists only as an extrapolation from 12,000 households.

drills.title: Two Stories Fit
drills.prompt: Paid conversions fell from 30% to 27% while traffic grew 60%. The team blames the new pricing page. Do you agree?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Course funnel (F6)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) reads both upper rates rather than one, registration 35.00% to 27.50%, down 7.50 percentage points, and payment 30.00% to 26.93%, down 3.07 percentage points, and notes that completion held at 30.00% in both years; (2) declines to treat the pricing page as established and grounds the refusal in the data rather than in an assumption about where the page sits in the cascade: the same four stage counts are reproduced without any change to the offer, so the exhibit cannot single one cause out; (3) names that second explanation, dilution of traffic by new channels, 3 to 7, with views up 100,000 to 160,000, +60.00%; (4) demonstrates it arithmetically instead of asserting it: holding the original 100,000 views at FY2023 behaviour, 35,000 registrations and 10,500 payments, the added 60,000 views give 44,000 - 35,000 = 9,000 registrations, 9,000 / 60,000 = 15.00%, and 11,850 - 10,500 = 1,350 payments, 1,350 / 9,000 = 15.00%, both positive; (5) states that the exhibit does not favour either explanation, since the printed 27.50% and 26.93% are the blended result under both; (6) names a test that separates them and states both outcomes: split the funnel by traffic source, where the offer story predicts lower rates in the original three channels as well, while the dilution story predicts the original three still at 35.00% and 30.00% with the shortfall confined to the four new channels; (7) does not stop at a single explanation and does not place the problem at the payment step alone, given that the registration rate fell by more. Bonus, not required for credit: notes that absolute counts rose at every stage, payments 10,500 to 11,850 and completions 3,150 to 3,555, both +12.86%, so falling rates are not a falling business; or that end-to-end conversion went 10,500 / 100,000 = 10.50% to 11,850 / 160,000 = 7.41%.

reference.en:
- Naive: the paid conversion rate fell, the pricing page is new, and the fall shows up on the payment step. The story fits, the team already believes it, and the funnel does not visibly argue back. One plausible cause arrives and the thinking stops there.
- Correct: two rates fell, not one. Registration went 35.00% to 27.50%, down 7.50 percentage points, and payment went 30.00% to 26.93%, down 3.07 percentage points. Completion did not move at all, 30.00% in both years. So whatever happened, most of it happened before anyone reached a price, and none of it touched the experience of people who paid.
- Note what the exhibit does not say. It gives the cascade as view, registration, payment, completion, and it never states where the pricing page sits inside it. So "the page cannot have affected registration" is an assumption about the product, not a reading of the data, and the case against the team's story has to be built from the numbers themselves.
- The same numbers support a second account just as well. Suppose the offer did not change and the traffic did: views grew 100,000 to 160,000, +60.00%, and acquisition channels went 3 to 7. If the original 100,000 views still behave as in FY2023, 35,000 registrations and 10,500 payments, then the added 60,000 views produced 44,000 - 35,000 = 9,000 registrations, a rate of 9,000 / 60,000 = 15.00%, and 11,850 - 10,500 = 1,350 payments, a rate of 1,350 / 9,000 = 15.00%. Both are positive and both are ordinary for cold traffic. Every printed count is reproduced without touching the product.
- So there are two accounts of one funnel. Under the offer story a single population converts worse, at 27.50% and 26.93%. Under the dilution story two populations, one unchanged and one weaker at 15.00% on each step, blend to exactly those same rates. The exhibit cannot choose between them, because the rates it prints are the blend, and the blend is all it prints.
- The spend line is consistent with dilution without settling it. The marketing budget went $2.4M to $4.6M, up 91.67%, to buy 60.00% more views: $2.4M over 100,000 views is $24.00 each, $4.6M over 160,000 views is $28.75. Paying more per view while opening four more channels is what buying further down the quality curve looks like, and it is equally what a more expensive auction looks like.
- What did not move is as informative as what did. NPS among completers is 44 against 43 and the average ticket held at $240, so nothing suggests the product or the price point degraded for the people who bought.
- The absolute counts rose at every stage. Payments went 10,500 to 11,850 and completions 3,150 to 3,555, both +12.86%, which at an unchanged $240 ticket is 10,500 x $240 = $2.52M against 11,850 x $240 = $2.844M. End to end the funnel did get thinner, 10,500 / 100,000 = 10.50% to 11,850 / 160,000 = 7.41%, but more people paid than last year. That changes how urgent this is, not whether it is real.
- Last mile: do not agree yet, and say why in three moves. First, the fall in the paid rate does not establish the pricing page: the same four stage counts are reproduced exactly, with the offer untouched, by traffic whose mix changed, and the larger of the two falls, registration 35.00% to 27.50%, sits at a step the team is not talking about. Second, the live alternative is sample selection, channels going 3 to 7 with new traffic converting near 15.00% on both steps, which lands on 44,000 registrations and 11,850 payments precisely. Third, the test that separates them is a funnel split by traffic source: if the offer worsened, registration and payment rates fall in the original three channels too; if the traffic was diluted, those three still run at 35.00% and 30.00% and the entire shortfall sits in the four new channels. Run that cut before anyone rewrites the pricing page, because the two stories prescribe opposite actions and only one of them is worth paying for.

drills.title: In That Order
drills.prompt: The ops director reads the chart as a chain: automation cut labour, which enabled the yield gain, which lifted margin. Does the exhibit support that reading?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Gross margin bridge, FY2023 → FY2024 (pp)

lines: *Note: the order of the factors in the bridge was set by the report's analyst; the chronology of the initiatives is not shown in the exhibit.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) answers the question directly — the exhibit does not support the ops director's reading — rather than endorsing the chain in whole or in part; (2) states that a waterfall shows contributions to a change and not a sequence of events, and cites the note that the order of the factors was set by the report's analyst while no chronology appears anywhere in the exhibit; (3) names at least one factor that the chain cannot absorb — raw material prices +1.2 pp or logistics -0.9 pp — and says the exhibit shows no link between it and the automation programme; (4) uses percentage points for the bridge, total +6.0 pp against margin 18.0% to 24.0%, and does not describe the move as a 6.0% rise; (5) brings the cost column into the answer: line automation cost $18.0M of the $24.8M total for +2.4 of the +6.0 pp, while lower labour cost delivered +1.8 pp at an initiative cost of $0.0M; (6) does not treat the first bar as the driver of the ones after it, and does not assign the labour saving to automation as established fact. Bonus, not required for credit: prices the effect, $18.0M / 2.4 = $7.50M per percentage point for automation against $4.2M / 1.5 = $2.80M for higher product yield; or names what would settle the causal question, namely implementation dates and an explicit basis for attributing the labour saving; or notes that logistics is the only negative bar, -0.9 pp, and carries $2.6M of spend.

reference.en:
- Naive: the bridge runs left to right and the factors are numbered 1 to 5, so it reads as a sequence: line automation +2.4, which produced lower labour cost +1.8, which enabled higher product yield +1.5. A waterfall is drawn as a chain of blocks handing height to each other, and numbering the blocks makes the chain look like a timeline.
- Correct: a waterfall orders contributions, not events, and here the ordering rule is visible on the face of the chart. The bars run +2.4, +1.8, +1.5, +1.2, then -0.9: strict descending order of size, the four positives first and the single negative last. Size of contribution is the only rule the sequence obeys, and the note under the table confirms it from the other side — the order was set by the report's analyst, and the exhibit carries no dates, no start months and no implementation sequence anywhere. So the question to put to the ops director is not what the chart shows but what it is sorted by: a chain of causes has no reason to arrive in descending order of magnitude, and a ranking by magnitude has no reason to be a chain. The bars descend because that is how the analyst laid them out, and the causal story is something the reader supplies.
- Two of the five bars cannot be fitted into the chain at all. Raw material prices +1.2 pp and logistics -0.9 pp are purchasing and freight outcomes; the exhibit shows no link between either of them and the automation programme, yet they sit in the same numbered column as if they were steps of it. Any reading that treats position as causation has to explain why those two are in the list.
- What the exhibit does support is an attribution in money. Line automation cost $18.0M of the $24.8M spent across all initiatives, or 72.58% of the money, and delivered +2.4 of the +6.0 pp, or 40.00% of the effect. That is $18.0M / 2.4 = $7.50M per percentage point. Higher product yield cost $4.2M for +1.5 pp, or $4.2M / 1.5 = $2.80M per percentage point — the cheaper buy by a wide margin. Lower labour cost delivered +1.8 pp, 30.00% of the change, at an initiative cost of $0.0M.
- The comparison only stands if labour is a separate factor, and that is exactly what the ops director denies. Take his version seriously for a moment: if the labour saving were an effect of the automation line, automation would carry +2.4 + 1.8 = +4.2 pp for the same $18.0M, which is $18.0M / 4.2 = $4.29M per percentage point, and the ranking against yield narrows without reversing. The exhibit gives no basis for making that transfer, so it stays a hypothesis, not a finding — but it does show what is at stake in the question.
- Note also that logistics is the only negative bar, -0.9 pp, and it carries $2.6M of spend. Whatever was bought there did not show up in margin over this period.
- Last mile: margin rose +6.0 pp, 18.0% to 24.0%, and the bridge accounts for that total exactly, but it does not establish any chain between the factors — so the ops director's reading is not supported by this exhibit. The decision he actually faces, whether to fund the next automation line, needs two things this chart cannot give: the implementation dates of each initiative, and a basis for assigning the labour saving. As printed, $18.0M bought 40.00% of the change while a factor with $0.0M of initiative cost bought 30.00% of it, and that is the comparison to put in front of him before any further capital is committed.

drills.title: Out of What
drills.prompt: Finance projects net revenue by taking gross revenue less the return rate. What number do you get, and is their method right?

blocks.title: Exhibit A — Order funnel, FY2024 (F6)
Exhibit B — Order economics

lines: *Note: the average ticket of a **returned** order is **$129** — returns are concentrated in the upper price range.*

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) builds the order count from the funnel rather than assuming it — 4,800,000 x 20.00% = 960,000, x 30.00% = 288,000 orders — and gets gross revenue as 288,000 x $86 = $24,768,000; (2) states that the 12.0% return rate is a share of orders, not of revenue, so gross revenue cannot be multiplied by it, and converts it to units: 288,000 x 12.0% = 34,560 orders; (3) uses the note's returned-order ticket of $129 rather than the $86 average, giving 34,560 x $129 = $4,458,240 of returned value; (4) answers with net revenue of $20,309,760 and rejects the $21,795,840 the finance method produces; (5) says the finance method is wrong in this case and names the condition under which it would be right — the return rate would have to be expressed in money, not in units; (6) quantifies the consequence, either as the $1,486,080 overstatement, or 7.32%, or by stating that returns are 18.00% of gross revenue against 12.00% of orders; (7) does not dismiss the return rate as too small to matter. Bonus, not required for credit: derives the 18.00% from the ticket ratio, $129 / $86 = 1.50 and 12.00% x 1.50 = 18.00%; or flags that returns are concentrated in the upper price range and that targeting expensive lines beats cutting the overall rate; or notes that repeat buyer share of 41% and delivery cost of $7.20 per order do not enter this calculation.

reference.en:
- Naive: the return rate is printed as 12.0% one row below gross revenue, so the two get multiplied together: $24,768,000 x 0.88 = $21,795,840 of net revenue. Finance states the method that way, and the arithmetic of the multiplication is correct — the input is not.
- Correct: the 12.0% is a share of orders, and the funnel is what supplies the orders. Visits 4,800,000 x 20.00% = 960,000 baskets, x 30.00% = 288,000 orders, and 288,000 x $86 = $24,768,000 of gross revenue. Returns are then 288,000 x 12.0% = 34,560 orders. To turn 34,560 orders into dollars you need the price of a returned order, and the note gives it: $129, not the $86 average. So 34,560 x $129 = $4,458,240, and net revenue is $24,768,000 - $4,458,240 = $20,309,760.
- The gap between the two answers is the whole point of the note. In money, returns are $4,458,240 / $24,768,000 = 18.00% of gross revenue against 12.00% of orders. The two figures differ by 6.00 percentage points and neither is wrong: they measure different things. The ratio between them is the ticket ratio, $129 / $86 = 1.50, and 12.00% x 1.50 = 18.00% recovers it exactly.
- Sized against the correct answer, finance overstates net revenue by $21,795,840 - $20,309,760 = $1,486,080, which is 7.32% of the correct $20,309,760. On a plan built off this line that is a shortfall large enough to move a hiring or inventory decision, and it arrives with no visible error anywhere in the model — every number in the calculation is a number that appears on the page.
- The rule finance is applying, gross x (1 - return rate), is not wrong in general. It holds whenever the return rate is expressed in money. Applied to a rate expressed in units it silently assumes that returned orders carry the average ticket, and here that assumption is the one thing the exhibit explicitly denies.
- Two rows invite work and do not belong to this question. Repeat buyer share of 41% and delivery cost of $7.20 per order describe the economics of orders that are kept and shipped; neither enters the bridge from gross to net revenue, and the baskets stage of the funnel matters only as the step that produces the order count.
- Last mile: net revenue is $20,309,760, not the $21,795,840 finance projects, because the return rate is measured in units while returned orders carry a $129 ticket against a fleet average of $86 — a $1,486,080 overstatement, or 7.32%. Correct the projection first, then take the second point to the merchandising team: returns are concentrated in the upper price range, so 18.00% of revenue is at stake against a 12.0% unit rate, and pulling the return rate down on the expensive lines is worth several times what the same reduction is worth on the average order.

drills.title: Mix or Merit
drills.prompt: Gross margin improved from 12.7% to 18.2%. The COO credits the operational excellence programme. Is that where it came from?

exhibit.title: Exhibit A — Gross margin bridge by segment ($M, pp)

checklist.en: Credit if ALL: (1) compares margins segment by segment across the two years and states that all three fell — Specialty 32.0% to 30.0%, Industrial 14.0% to 13.0%, Commodity 6.0% to 5.0%; (2) notes total revenue is unchanged at $1,200M in both years, so the aggregate improvement cannot be attributed to growth; (3) produces the decomposition with both quantities and closes the identity: mix +6.90 pp, rate -1.40 pp, summing to the actual +5.50 pp — asserting that mix mattered without both figures does not earn this point; (4) identifies the mix shift in the weights: Specialty 15.0% to 40.0% and Commodity 50.0% to 20.0%; (5) answers the COO directly with a no — the operational excellence programme is not where the margin improvement came from; (6) uses percentage points for the bridge and does not restate the move as a 5.50% rise; (7) does not credit the gain to Specialty performing better, given that Specialty's own margin fell 32.0% to 30.0%. Bonus, not required for credit: cross-checks by applying FY2023 rates to FY2024 revenue, 480 x 32.0% + 480 x 14.0% + 240 x 6.0% = $235.20M, or 19.60% of $1,200M, which is 12.70 + 6.90; or converts to money, profit $152.40M to $218.40M, +$66.00M; or raises repeatability, with Commodity already down to 20.0%; or reads the even 1 to 2 point rate declines as general price pressure rather than a single failing line.

reference.en:
- Naive: gross margin went 12.70% to 18.20%, the bridge accounts for the whole move, and the operational excellence programme ran across the same period, so the COO signs off on his own explanation. The aggregate did improve and nothing in the total contradicts him.
- Correct: compare the segments year on year before touching the total, and every single margin fell. Specialty 32.0% to 30.0%, Industrial 14.0% to 13.0%, Commodity 6.0% to 5.0%. Total revenue is identical in both years, $1,200M against $1,200M, so nothing here was bought with growth either. Operations got worse in all three lines while the company-level margin rose 5.50 percentage points.
- The reconciliation is a two-part decomposition, and the bridge shows the two parts without showing how they were built. Mix, holding FY2023 rates and moving the weights: (0.40 - 0.15) x 32 + (0.40 - 0.35) x 14 + (0.20 - 0.50) x 6 = +6.90 pp. Rate, holding FY2024 weights and moving the rates: (30 - 32) x 0.40 + (13 - 14) x 0.40 + (5 - 6) x 0.20 = -1.40 pp. Together +6.90 - 1.40 = +5.50 pp, which is the actual move exactly, with no residual to explain away.
- The same result arrives from the other direction as a check. Apply the old rates to the new revenue: 480 x 32.0% + 480 x 14.0% + 240 x 6.0% = $235.20M, which is 19.60% of $1,200M and equals 12.70 + 6.90. The company actually earned 18.20%, so the rate deterioration cost 1.40 pp of margin that the mix shift had already delivered.
- The mix shift is a portfolio move, not a performance one. Specialty revenue went $180M to $480M, +$300M and a factor of 2.67, Industrial $420M to $480M, +$60M, and Commodity $600M to $240M, -$360M. Weights went Specialty 15.0% to 40.0% and Commodity 50.0% to 20.0% while the top line stood still — the company sold a different set of products, not the same products better. In money the profit pool went $152.40M to $218.40M, +$66.00M, and 5.50% of $1,200M is that same $66.00M.
- The rate declines are worth a second look for what they are not. They land at 2, 1 and 1 percentage points across three very different product lines, and that evenness looks more like general price pressure than like a failure in one operation. It is also the one thing an excellence programme was supposed to prevent, and it did not.
- Last mile: margin rose +5.50 pp, of which mix contributed +6.90 pp and rate took away -1.40 pp, so the operational excellence programme is not where the improvement came from — on the evidence it did not stop the erosion it was meant to stop. The gain was purchased by walking out of Commodity, and the question for the COO is whether that trade can be repeated, because Commodity is down to 20.0% of $1,200M with the exits already taken. Before the next planning cycle, ask what the FY2025 margin looks like if the mix stops moving and the rates keep falling 1 to 2 points a year.
